**HARGROVE, SIMMONS & LOCKE LLP** *Attorneys at Law*

One Federal Street, 30th Floor Boston, MA 02110

Washington, D.C. \| Boston \| San Francisco

CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED

June 27, 2025

Sarah Kowalski Vice President, Regulatory Affairs Pinnacle Therapeutics, Inc. 245 Binney Street, Suite 1200 Cambridge, MA 02142

**Re: Engagement Letter --- Regulatory Gap Analysis of Clinical Trial Protocol PTX-4820-201 (Version 3.0) in Support of Investigational New Drug Application Submission for PTX-4820**

Dear Ms. Kowalski:

**[I. Introduction and Engagement Confirmation]{.underline}**

On behalf of Hargrove, Simmons & Locke LLP (\"HSL\" or the \"Firm\"), I am pleased to confirm the terms under which HSL will perform a regulatory gap analysis of the clinical trial protocol described below on behalf of Pinnacle Therapeutics, Inc. (\"Pinnacle\" or the \"Company\"). We appreciate the Company\'s continued confidence in the Firm and are grateful for the opportunity to assist Pinnacle at this important stage in its regulatory strategy.

As you know, HSL has represented Pinnacle since the Company\'s Series B financing round in 2021, and we have served as Pinnacle\'s primary outside regulatory counsel throughout that period. This engagement letter supplements the existing Master Engagement Agreement between HSL and Pinnacle, dated September 14, 2021, as amended (the \"MEA\"). In the event of any conflict between this letter and the MEA, the terms of this letter shall govern with respect to the specific engagement described herein; all other provisions of the MEA remain in full force and effect.

This engagement is being undertaken in connection with Pinnacle\'s planned Investigational New Drug (\"IND\") application submission for PTX-4820, the Company\'s novel dual GLP-1/GVP receptor agonist, which is being developed for the treatment of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (\"NASH\") with liver fibrosis (stage F2 or F3). We understand that PTX-4820 received Orphan Drug Designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (\"FDA\") on November 8, 2024 (Designation No. 24-5773), and that Pinnacle\'s target date for IND submission is September 15, 2025. We further understand that Pinnacle currently has one active IND on file with FDA --- IND No. 152847 for PTX-3100 (a Type 2 diabetes candidate currently in Phase 1 clinical trials) --- and that the PTX-4820 IND will represent the Company\'s second IND submission.

The protocol under review --- Clinical Trial Protocol PTX-4820-201, Version 3.0, dated May 18, 2025 (the \"Protocol\") --- was initially drafted by Pinnacle\'s contract research organization, Trident Clinical Research Organization (\"Trident CRO\"), under Pinnacle\'s direction and oversight. The purpose of this engagement is to perform a comprehensive regulatory gap analysis of the Protocol, including its appended Informed Consent Form template, to identify any gaps, deficiencies, or areas of non-compliance with applicable regulatory requirements, FDA guidance, and the specific recommendations provided by FDA during the Pre-IND meeting process, as described more fully below.

**[II. Scope of Work]{.underline}**

The following sections describe in detail the scope of the regulatory gap analysis to be performed by HSL.

**A. Documents to Be Reviewed**

HSL will review the following documents in connection with this engagement:

1\. **Clinical Trial Protocol PTX-4820-201, Version 3.0**, dated May 18, 2025, including all appendices thereto. This review will specifically include the Informed Consent Form (\"ICF\") template appended to the Protocol as Appendix A, which will be reviewed on a line-by-line basis against applicable regulatory requirements as described below.

2\. **FDA Pre-IND Meeting (Type B) Written Minutes**, dated April 2, 2025, from the Pre-IND meeting held on March 12, 2025, with the Division of Hepatology and Nutrition (\"DHN\"), Office of Immunology and Inflammation, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (\"CDER\") (the \"Pre-IND Meeting Minutes\"). These minutes memorialize FDA\'s specific recommendations regarding the design and content of the Protocol, and will serve as a primary benchmark against which the Protocol will be assessed.

3\. **Additional Pinnacle Internal Documents and Correspondence.** HSL will review any additional internal Pinnacle documents, memoranda, or correspondence relevant to the regulatory strategy for PTX-4820-201 that Pinnacle makes available to the Firm during the engagement period.

In addition to the foregoing, HSL will prepare and utilize an internal regulatory requirements checklist (the \"Regulatory Requirements Checklist\") that cross-references all applicable regulations, guidance documents, and FDA meeting recommendations against the specific sections and provisions of the Protocol. This checklist will serve as a systematic working tool throughout the review and will be delivered to Pinnacle in completed form as part of the final deliverables.

**B. Regulatory Standards Against Which Protocol Will Be Assessed**

The Protocol will be assessed against the following regulatory authorities, regulations, and guidance documents, which together establish the applicable benchmark for compliance:

1\. **21 CFR Part 312** --- Investigational New Drug Application requirements, including the IND content and format requirements set forth in 21 CFR 312.23(a)(6) (protocol requirements for Phase 2 protocols), safety reporting obligations under 21 CFR 312.32 (IND safety reporting), and the general requirements for clinical investigations under Parts 312.50 through 312.70.

2\. **21 CFR Part 50** --- Protection of Human Subjects, with specific focus on the informed consent requirements set forth in 21 CFR 50.25(a) (basic elements of informed consent, including the eight required elements) and 21 CFR 50.25(b) (additional elements of informed consent, including the six additional elements that must be provided when appropriate). The Protocol\'s ICF template will be reviewed against these requirements on an element-by-element basis to confirm completeness and accuracy.

3\. **21 CFR Part 56** --- Institutional Review Boards, including requirements pertaining to IRB review and approval of the Protocol and ICF, continuing review, and reporting obligations.

4\. **21 CFR Part 11** --- Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures, including the applicability of Part 11 requirements to the electronic data capture (\"EDC\") system to be used in the clinical trial (TrialVault, operated by Trident CRO), and the Protocol\'s provisions, if any, addressing compliance with Part 11 for electronic source data, audit trail requirements, system validation, and electronic signature authentication.

5\. **ICH E6(R2)** --- Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, as adopted by FDA, including sponsor responsibilities, investigator responsibilities, essential document requirements, and clinical trial protocol content requirements.

6\. **ICH M3(R2)** --- Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human Clinical Trials and Marketing Authorization for Pharmaceuticals, including the requirements for reproductive toxicity studies (embryo-fetal development studies, fertility studies) that must be completed or in progress to support the enrollment of women of childbearing potential in clinical trials, and the corresponding requirements for contraception and pregnancy testing in the clinical protocol.

7\. **ICH E9(R1)** --- Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials: Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis (May 2021), including the estimand framework and its application to the Protocol\'s interim analysis design, primary endpoint definition, and sensitivity analysis plan.

8\. **FDA Guidance for Industry: \"Noncirrhotic Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH) with Liver Fibrosis: Developing Drugs for Treatment\"** (December 2018), including FDA\'s recommendations regarding appropriate clinical trial endpoints, patient populations, histological assessment standards, and trial design considerations for NASH drug development.

9\. **FDA Guidance for Industry: \"Adaptive Designs for Clinical Trials of Drugs and Biologics\"** (November 2019), including FDA\'s recommendations regarding the design, implementation, and statistical analysis of adaptive features in clinical trial protocols, and the pre-specification of adaptation rules.

10\. **FDA Guidance for Industry: \"Safety Reporting Requirements for INDs and BA/BE Studies\"** (December 2012), including the requirements for expedited reporting of IND safety reports, the applicable reporting timelines (7-day and 15-day calendar day requirements), and the definitions and criteria for \"suspected adverse reaction,\" \"unexpected adverse reaction,\" and \"serious adverse event\" as applied to safety reporting obligations.

11\. **FDA Written Recommendations from the March 12, 2025 Pre-IND Meeting** as memorialized in the Pre-IND Meeting Minutes dated April 2, 2025. The Protocol will be systematically compared against each specific recommendation made by the Division of Hepatology and Nutrition, including but not limited to recommendations regarding the Data Safety Monitoring Board (\"DSMB\") structure and charter requirements, dose-escalation and dose-titration schemes, exclusion criteria (including Model for End-Stage Liver Disease or \"MELD\" score thresholds), stopping criteria, interim analysis design and timing, and centralized pathology review design and procedures.

12\. **Regulatory Requirements of Non-U.S. Jurisdictions.** Because the Protocol contemplates clinical trial sites in both the United States and Canada, the gap analysis will also assess the Protocol\'s compliance with Health Canada regulatory requirements, including the *Food and Drug Regulations* (Division 5 --- Drugs for Clinical Trials Involving Human Subjects) and Clinical Trial Application (\"CTA\") requirements applicable to the six (6) Canadian sites identified in the Protocol. The assessment will identify any areas where the Protocol, as currently drafted, may fail to satisfy Canadian regulatory requirements or may require supplemental provisions for the Canadian sites.

**C. Specific Areas of Analysis**

Within the framework described above, HSL will conduct the following specific analytical tasks:

1\. **Protocol-to-Meeting-Minutes Comparison.** HSL will perform a systematic, recommendation-by-recommendation comparison of all FDA Pre-IND Meeting recommendations memorialized in the April 2, 2025 minutes against the corresponding provisions of the current Protocol. The purpose of this comparison is to identify any deviations from, partial implementations of, or outright omissions of FDA\'s stated recommendations. This analysis will specifically encompass FDA\'s recommendations regarding DSMB requirements (including charter provisions and independence criteria), dose-escalation and dose-titration schemes, patient exclusion criteria (including the recommended MELD score threshold), stopping criteria (including hepatotoxicity stopping rules), interim analysis design (including timing and statistical methodology), and centralized pathology review design and operational procedures.

2\. **Informed Consent Form Review.** HSL will conduct a line-by-line review of the ICF template appended as Appendix A to the Protocol. This review will assess the ICF against the required elements of informed consent set forth in 21 CFR 50.25(a) and 50.25(b) to confirm that all required elements are present and adequately disclosed. The review will also verify that all factual statements contained in the ICF --- including statements regarding study duration, procedures, number of visits, potential risks, and available alternatives --- accurately reflect the corresponding provisions of the Protocol itself. We note your specific request that we pay particular attention to the ICF review, given recent instances in the industry where FDA has imposed clinical holds due to deficiencies in informed consent documentation. We will ensure the ICF analysis is thorough and granular.

3\. **Safety Reporting Provisions.** HSL will review the Protocol\'s safety reporting framework, including the definitions of adverse events, serious adverse events, and suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions (\"SUSARs\"), the specified reporting timelines, and the escalation procedures for safety signals, against the requirements of 21 CFR 312.32 and the December 2012 FDA guidance on safety reporting requirements for INDs. This review will assess the adequacy and regulatory compliance of the expedited reporting timelines specified in the Protocol for IND safety reports.

4\. **Data Integrity and Electronic Systems.** HSL will assess the Protocol\'s provisions, if any, regarding the electronic data capture system to be used in the trial --- specifically the TrialVault EDC platform operated by Trident CRO --- for compliance with 21 CFR Part 11. This assessment will consider whether the Protocol contains adequate provisions addressing system validation, audit trail functionality, electronic signature requirements, data backup and recovery, and access controls, as required for electronic records that are intended to serve as regulatory submissions or as part of the clinical trial record.

5\. **Subject Protection and Safety Provisions.** HSL will review the Protocol\'s provisions for the protection of trial subjects, including reproductive safety measures (pregnancy testing frequency and methodology, contraception requirements for both male and female participants of reproductive potential), protections for any vulnerable populations that may be enrolled, and the adequacy of risk disclosure in both the Protocol and the ICF. This analysis will be conducted with reference to ICH M3(R2) guidance on reproductive toxicity study timing and the corresponding contraception requirements, as well as the general subject protection standards of 21 CFR Part 50 and ICH E6(R2).

6\. **Multinational Regulatory Compliance.** HSL will assess whether the Protocol, as currently drafted, adequately addresses the regulatory requirements for all participating jurisdictions. Given that the Protocol contemplates operation at both U.S. and Canadian clinical trial sites, particular attention will be paid to whether the Protocol includes the necessary provisions, disclosures, and procedural safeguards to support a Clinical Trial Application submission to Health Canada for the six Canadian sites, or whether supplemental provisions or country-specific addenda may be required.

7\. **Statistical Design Review.** HSL will review the Protocol\'s provisions regarding interim analysis timing, the specified alpha-spending methodology (including the O\'Brien-Fleming spending function or any other approach referenced in the Protocol), futility analysis provisions, and sample size calculations against the recommendations made by FDA during the Pre-IND Meeting and the applicable principles set forth in ICH E9(R1) and the November 2019 FDA adaptive designs guidance.

**[III. Deliverables]{.underline}**

HSL will deliver the following work product to Pinnacle in connection with this engagement:

1\. **Regulatory Gap Analysis Memorandum.** A comprehensive written memorandum identifying all gaps, deficiencies, and areas of non-compliance identified in the Protocol and the appended ICF template. Each identified issue will be categorized by severity level --- Critical, Major, or Minor --- based on the potential regulatory impact and the likelihood that the issue could result in a refusal to file, clinical hold, or FDA enforcement action. For each identified issue, the memorandum will include a detailed description of the deficiency, a citation to the applicable regulatory authority or guidance, an explanation of the regulatory risk, and a specific recommended remediation, including proposed protocol or ICF language where appropriate. The memorandum will include an executive summary suitable for distribution to Pinnacle\'s senior leadership team.

2\. **Completed Regulatory Requirements Checklist.** A filled-in version of the Regulatory Requirements Checklist described in Section II.A above, cross-referencing each applicable regulatory requirement against the corresponding section of the Protocol and noting the compliance status (Compliant, Non-Compliant, Partially Compliant, or Not Addressed) for each item.

3\. **Oral Briefing.** A briefing call with Pinnacle\'s regulatory affairs team to walk through the findings of the gap analysis, discuss remediation priorities, and answer questions regarding the recommended protocol amendments. This briefing will be scheduled at a mutually convenient time following delivery of the written memorandum.

All written deliverables will be provided to Pinnacle no later than **July 11, 2025**, which is two weeks from the date of this engagement letter. This timeline is designed to support Pinnacle\'s target IND submission date of September 15, 2025, and to allow adequate time for the Company to implement any necessary protocol amendments, obtain updated IRB approvals, and finalize the IND submission package.

**[IV. HSL Team Composition]{.underline}**

The following HSL attorneys will be assigned to this engagement:

**Thomas Kelling, Partner** (Boston office) --- Mr. Kelling will serve as the Engagement Partner and primary point of contact for this matter. Mr. Kelling specializes in FDA regulatory matters and has advised pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies on IND submissions, NDA and BLA filings, pre-approval inspections, and FDA enforcement matters for over fifteen years. He has served as Pinnacle\'s primary outside regulatory counsel since 2021 and has detailed familiarity with the Company\'s regulatory history and pipeline strategy.

**Diana Forsythe, Partner** (Washington, D.C. office) --- Ms. Forsythe, who leads HSL\'s Life Sciences Regulatory Practice Group, will provide senior oversight and quality review of the gap analysis memorandum and all deliverables. Given the significance of the PTX-4820 IND submission to Pinnacle\'s overall pipeline strategy, Ms. Forsythe\'s involvement will ensure that the analysis benefits from the broadest available regulatory perspective within the Firm.

**Priya Mehta, Associate** (Boston office, fifth year) --- Ms. Mehta will conduct the primary regulatory review of the Protocol and ICF, prepare the Regulatory Requirements Checklist, and draft the gap analysis memorandum. Ms. Mehta has substantial experience in IND and NDA regulatory submissions and has been involved in prior HSL engagements for Pinnacle, including work on the PTX-3100 IND filing.

The team may consult with other HSL attorneys as needed during the course of this engagement, including attorneys with expertise in Canadian pharmaceutical regulation to support the Health Canada compliance analysis for the Canadian trial sites.

**[V. Client Contacts and Coordination]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s primary contact for this engagement will be **Sarah Kowalski, Vice President of Regulatory Affairs**. In addition, HSL may coordinate with the following Pinnacle personnel as needed during the course of the review:

> • **Dr. Rajiv Anand, Chief Medical Officer**, for clinical and medical questions regarding the Protocol design, safety parameters, and the therapeutic context for PTX-4820;
>
> • **Dr. Margaret Yuen, Chief Executive Officer**, as needed for strategic matters relating to the IND submission timeline and Pinnacle\'s overall development plan; and
>
> • **Dr. Caroline Xu, Project Lead at Trident CRO**, for questions regarding the operational sections of the Protocol, the TrialVault electronic data capture system, CRO procedures, and site-level implementation matters.

We respectfully request that Pinnacle provide to HSL any additional protocol-related documents, correspondence with FDA, or internal memoranda that may be relevant to this analysis within three (3) business days of the date of this letter, to ensure that our review is based on the most complete available record.

**[VI. Fees and Billing Arrangements]{.underline}**

This engagement will be billed on an hourly basis in accordance with the Firm\'s standard rate schedule, as set forth in the MEA. Partners and associates assigned to this matter will bill at their current standard rates. Based on the anticipated scope of work described in this letter, HSL estimates that total professional fees for this engagement will be in the range of **\$320,000 to \$420,000**. This estimate is based on the scope as currently defined and the documents currently identified for review.

If during the course of our analysis additional issues arise that require expanded analysis beyond the scope described herein --- for example, significant or complex regulatory questions related to the Canadian trial sites, the need to analyze additional FDA guidance documents not enumerated above, or the discovery of issues requiring in-depth analysis beyond what is typically expected in an engagement of this nature --- HSL will promptly notify Pinnacle before incurring fees in excess of the estimated range, and the parties will discuss the expanded scope and any revised estimate before additional work is undertaken.

Invoices will be rendered monthly and are payable within thirty (30) days of the invoice date. Out-of-pocket expenses, including legal research database access fees, document reproduction costs, and travel expenses (if any), will be billed at cost.

Please note that this fee estimate does not include any subsequent work to draft protocol amendments, prepare revised ICF language, assist with the preparation or assembly of the IND submission package, or provide representation before FDA (including responding to information requests or clinical hold letters). Any such additional services would be scoped and agreed upon separately.

**[VII. Limitations and Disclaimers]{.underline}**

The regulatory gap analysis to be performed under this engagement is a legal and regulatory review of the Protocol and the appended ICF template. It does not constitute, and should not be construed as, medical, scientific, or clinical advice. HSL will not independently verify preclinical data, clinical data, pharmacokinetic data, or any other scientific data referenced in the Protocol; our analysis will assume the accuracy of such data as presented.

The analysis will be based on the regulations, guidance documents, and FDA policies in effect as of the date of the gap analysis memorandum. Subsequent changes in law, regulation, or FDA guidance, or the issuance of new FDA guidance documents, may affect the conclusions of our analysis. HSL\'s analysis represents the Firm\'s professional judgment based on our experience and understanding of FDA regulatory requirements and enforcement practices; however, FDA retains discretion in its review of IND submissions and may take positions that differ from HSL\'s assessment.

This engagement does not include representation before FDA, including but not limited to responding to FDA information requests, attending FDA meetings, or responding to refuse-to-file letters or clinical hold orders, unless separately agreed in writing. The gap analysis will focus on the regulatory compliance of the Protocol document and the appended ICF template; it will not encompass a review of other components of the IND submission package (e.g., the Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls sections, the Pharmacology/Toxicology sections, or the Investigator\'s Brochure) unless separately engaged to do so.

**[VIII. Confidentiality and Privilege]{.underline}**

All work product produced by HSL in connection with this engagement, including the Regulatory Gap Analysis Memorandum, the Regulatory Requirements Checklist, internal notes, and all related communications, is subject to the attorney-client privilege and the work product doctrine. HSL will maintain the confidentiality of all Pinnacle proprietary information provided to the Firm in connection with this engagement, including the Protocol, the Pre-IND Meeting Minutes, internal correspondence, and any other proprietary or confidential materials.

The gap analysis memorandum will be marked as \"Attorney-Client Privileged / Attorney Work Product\" and should be treated as such by all recipients. We advise Pinnacle not to share the memorandum or any other HSL work product with third parties --- including Trident CRO, the Ridgeway Institutional Review Board, or any other outside party --- without first consulting HSL regarding the potential for privilege waiver.

**[IX. Acceptance]{.underline}**

If the foregoing accurately reflects Pinnacle\'s understanding of the terms of this engagement, please countersign this letter in the space provided below and return an executed copy to my attention. Upon receipt of the countersigned letter, HSL will commence work immediately.

We look forward to working with you and the Pinnacle team on this important matter, and we appreciate the Company\'s continued confidence in Hargrove, Simmons & Locke LLP.

Sincerely,

HARGROVE, SIMMONS & LOCKE LLP

**[3.1 Meeting Request]{.underline}**

Pinnacle Therapeutics, Inc. (\"Pinnacle\" or \"the Sponsor\") requested a Type B pre-Investigational New Drug (pre-IND) meeting with the Division of Hepatology and Nutrition (DHN) to discuss the proposed Phase 2b clinical development plan for PTX-4820, a novel dual glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GVP) receptor agonist, in the treatment of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) with liver fibrosis. The Sponsor sought FDA input on the design, endpoints, safety monitoring framework, and statistical methodology of the proposed Phase 2b study (Protocol PTX-4820-201) prior to the submission of an Investigational New Drug application.

**[3.2 Compound Description]{.underline}**

PTX-4820 is a novel, long-acting dual GLP-1/GVP receptor agonist formulated for subcutaneous injection. PTX-4820 is a 39-amino acid synthetic peptide with a C18 fatty acid side chain modification to facilitate albumin binding and extend the circulating half-life, enabling once-weekly dosing. The proposed mechanism of action in NASH involves multiple complementary pathways: (a) reduction in hepatic de novo lipogenesis through improved insulin sensitivity and direct hepatocyte signaling; (b) anti-inflammatory effects mediated through reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) and modulation of hepatic macrophage activation; and (c) direct anti-fibrotic signaling through attenuation of hepatic stellate cell activation and collagen deposition. Preclinical data generated by Pinnacle in rodent models of NASH (diet-induced steatohepatitis in C57BL/6J mice and the STAM model) demonstrated dose-dependent reductions in hepatic steatosis, lobular inflammation, hepatocyte ballooning, and fibrosis stage after 12 weeks of treatment.

**[3.3 Regulatory History]{.underline}**

PTX-4820 received Orphan Drug Designation from the FDA on November 8, 2024, under Designation Number 24-5773, for the treatment of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis with liver fibrosis. Pinnacle has one prior IND on file with the Agency: IND 152847 for PTX-3100, a selective GLP-1 receptor agonist under investigation for the treatment of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is currently in a Phase 1 single ascending dose and multiple ascending dose study in healthy volunteers.

**[3.4 Nonclinical Development Status]{.underline}**

Pinnacle reported that it has completed 26-week Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) repeat-dose toxicology studies of PTX-4820 in Sprague-Dawley rats and cynomolgus monkeys, both of which were completed in December 2024. The key findings and no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs) from these studies were summarized in the meeting briefing package. The Sponsor indicated that the nonclinical safety profile supports initiation of clinical studies.

**[3.5 Purpose of the Meeting]{.underline}**

The Sponsor\'s stated purpose for the meeting was to obtain FDA feedback and recommendations on the proposed Phase 2b study design before IND submission, with a target IND submission date of September 15, 2025. Specifically, the Sponsor sought Division input on: (1) the acceptability of the primary endpoint; (2) the dose-ranging design and dose-titration scheme; (3) the proposed study population and key inclusion/exclusion criteria; (4) the need for an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board; (5) stopping rules and safety monitoring criteria; (6) the planned interim analysis; and (7) the adequacy of the nonclinical package to support the proposed 52-week clinical study.

**[3.6 Proposed Study Overview]{.underline}**

As described in the meeting briefing package, the proposed study (Protocol PTX-4820-201) is a Phase 2b, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, dose-ranging study of PTX-4820 in adults with histologically confirmed NASH and stage F2 or F3 liver fibrosis. The study is designed with four treatment arms: PTX-4820 5 mg subcutaneous once weekly (Arm A), PTX-4820 15 mg subcutaneous once weekly (Arm B), PTX-4820 30 mg subcutaneous once weekly (Arm C), and matched placebo subcutaneous once weekly (Arm D), with a 1:1:1:1 randomization ratio. The planned sample size is 360 subjects (90 per arm). The treatment duration is 52 weeks, with a paired liver biopsy at baseline and Week 52. The primary efficacy endpoint is the proportion of subjects achieving ≥1-stage improvement in liver fibrosis as assessed by the NASH Clinical Research Network (CRN) histological scoring system, with no worsening of NASH (defined as no increase in NAS for steatosis, lobular inflammation, or hepatocyte ballooning), at Week 52 compared to baseline. The study is planned to be conducted at approximately 28 clinical sites (22 in the United States and 6 in Canada), with estimated enrollment from October 2025 through October 2026.

**[Section 4: Sponsor\'s Questions and FDA Responses]{.underline}**

The Sponsor submitted seven questions to the Division as part of the meeting briefing package. The following sections document each question as posed by the Sponsor, the FDA\'s response, and any related discussion points. Where the Sponsor\'s briefing package contained proposals on specific study design elements, the FDA\'s response references those proposals directly.

**[4.1 Question 1 --- Primary Endpoint (Paired Liver Biopsy)]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division agree that paired liver biopsy at baseline and Week 52, with a primary endpoint of ≥1-stage improvement in fibrosis (NASH CRN scoring system) with no worsening of NASH, is an acceptable primary endpoint for the proposed Phase 2b study?\"

**FDA Response.** The Division agrees that paired liver biopsy at baseline and Week 52, with a primary endpoint of ≥1-stage improvement in fibrosis (NASH CRN scoring system) with no worsening of NASH, is an acceptable primary endpoint for a Phase 2b study in NASH with liver fibrosis. This endpoint is consistent with the FDA Guidance for Industry: *\"Noncirrhotic Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH) with Liver Fibrosis: Developing Drugs for Treatment\"* (December 2018), which identifies histological improvement in fibrosis without worsening of steatohepatitis as a basis for conditional approval. The Division considers histological endpoints assessed by paired liver biopsy to remain the standard for demonstrating treatment benefit in NASH clinical trials, and notes that a 52-week treatment duration is appropriate for assessing clinically meaningful changes in fibrosis stage.

The Division emphasizes that biopsy adequacy criteria should be prespecified in the protocol to minimize the risk of uninterpretable or inadequate biopsy specimens. Specifically, the protocol should require a minimum biopsy length of 1.5 cm and a minimum of 6 portal tracts for a biopsy specimen to be considered adequate for histological scoring. The protocol should also prespecify procedures for handling inadequate biopsy specimens, including whether repeat biopsy will be offered and the timeframe within which a repeat biopsy must be obtained.

The Division further notes that the NASH CRN histological scoring system is the accepted and validated scoring system for use in NASH clinical trials, and the Division agrees with the Sponsor\'s choice of this scoring system. The four components of the NAS (steatosis grade, lobular inflammation, hepatocyte ballooning, and fibrosis stage) should each be scored independently, and the protocol should clearly define what constitutes \"no worsening of NASH\" for the purposes of the composite primary endpoint.

With regard to the pathology review process, the Division has a strong recommendation. The Division strongly recommends that the Sponsor implement a centralized pathology reading panel consisting of at least two independent hepatopathologists for scoring of all biopsy specimens using the NASH CRN scoring system. In cases of disagreement between the two primary readers, adjudication by a third independent hepatopathologist should be performed. The Division notes that single-reader pathology assessment introduces unacceptable inter-reader variability and could compromise the reliability and regulatory acceptability of the primary endpoint assessment. Published literature on pathologist concordance in NASH histological scoring demonstrates that inter-reader variability in fibrosis staging can range from a kappa statistic of 0.50 to 0.70 for a single reader, which is insufficiently reliable for the primary efficacy assessment in a registration-enabling study design.

The Sponsor should prespecify the following elements relating to the centralized pathology review in the protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP): (a) the qualification criteria for the independent hepatopathologists serving on the reading panel; (b) the blinding procedures for pathologists, including blinding to treatment assignment, visit (baseline vs. Week 52), and the scores assigned by the other reader(s); (c) the criteria for invoking the third reader (i.e., the definition of \"disagreement\" between the two primary readers, such as any discordance in fibrosis stage or a difference of ≥2 points in total NAS); (d) the adjudication process and how the final consensus score will be determined; and (e) training and calibration procedures for the reading panel prior to the initiation of scoring. The Division considers these elements to be critical to the integrity of the primary efficacy assessment.

**[4.2 Question 2 --- Dose-Ranging Design and Titration]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division agree with the proposed dose-ranging design of PTX-4820 at 5 mg, 15 mg, and 30 mg administered subcutaneously once weekly, with a matched placebo arm, using a 1:1:1:1 randomization? Does the Division have recommendations regarding dose escalation for the higher dose arms?\"

**FDA Response.** The Division generally agrees with the proposed four-arm dose-ranging design (PTX-4820 5 mg, 15 mg, and 30 mg, and matched placebo) with a 1:1:1:1 randomization ratio. The Division considers this to be an appropriate design for a Phase 2b dose-ranging study. The dose range selected (spanning a 6-fold range from 5 mg to 30 mg) provides adequate separation to characterize the dose-response relationship for both efficacy and safety endpoints. The inclusion of a concurrent placebo arm is necessary and appropriate for a double-blind Phase 2b study in this therapeutic area. The 1:1:1:1 randomization ratio provides balanced allocation across arms, which the Division considers reasonable for this study design.

However, the Division expresses concern regarding the proposed dose-escalation scheme for the 30 mg dose arm (Arm C). As described in the Sponsor\'s meeting briefing package, the Sponsor proposed a 2-week titration schedule for the 30 mg arm: 5 mg at Week 1, 15 mg at Week 2, with escalation to the full 30 mg dose beginning at Week 3. Based on the well-characterized class effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists, gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events --- including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and decreased appetite --- are expected to be dose-dependent and represent the most common tolerability-limiting adverse effects for this drug class. Clinical experience with approved GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide, tirzepatide) has established that gradual dose titration over a period of several weeks is essential to mitigate the incidence and severity of GI adverse events and to minimize early discontinuations due to intolerability.

The Division recommends a titration period of at least 4 weeks for subjects randomized to the 30 mg dose arm to reduce the incidence and severity of GI adverse events and minimize early discontinuations that could compromise the interpretability of the dose-response relationship. The Division suggests a titration schedule such as the following, or a similar stepwise escalation over a minimum of 4 weeks:

> • Week 1: 5 mg subcutaneous once weekly
>
> • Week 2: 10 mg subcutaneous once weekly
>
> • Week 3: 15 mg subcutaneous once weekly
>
> • Week 4 onward: 30 mg subcutaneous once weekly

The Sponsor\'s proposed 2-week titration schedule (5 mg at Week 1, 15 mg at Week 2, 30 mg from Week 3 onward) is considered insufficient by the Division. The Division notes that an inadequate titration period could result in disproportionately high dropout rates in the 30 mg arm relative to the other treatment arms, introducing differential attrition bias and potentially compromising the interpretability of the dose-response relationship that is the primary objective of this Phase 2b study. Furthermore, high early dropout rates due to GI intolerability in the 30 mg arm could undermine the statistical power of the study for the highest dose group, which is likely to be of greatest interest for dose selection in Phase 3.

The Division also notes that the lower dose arms (5 mg and 15 mg) may not require formal dose titration, as the anticipated GI adverse events at these dose levels may be tolerable without gradual escalation. However, the Sponsor may wish to consider implementing a titration scheme for the 15 mg arm (e.g., 5 mg at Week 1, 15 mg from Week 2 onward) to further reduce early GI events and maintain blinding integrity across arms. The Division does not require titration for the 15 mg arm but considers it a reasonable option for the Sponsor\'s consideration.

The Division recommends that the titration scheme be clearly described in the protocol with specific dose levels, timing, and criteria for dose escalation. The protocol should also address management of GI adverse events during the titration period, including whether dose reduction or temporary dose delay will be permitted and under what circumstances.

**[4.3 Question 3 --- Study Population and Exclusion Criteria]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division agree with the proposed inclusion and exclusion criteria, including enrollment of adults aged 18--75 with histologically confirmed NASH and stage F2 or F3 liver fibrosis?\"

**FDA Response.** The Division generally agrees with the proposed study population as described in the Sponsor\'s meeting briefing package. Enrollment of subjects with histologically confirmed NASH and stage F2 or F3 liver fibrosis (as assessed by the NASH CRN scoring system) is consistent with the FDA Guidance for Industry: *\"Noncirrhotic Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH) with Liver Fibrosis: Developing Drugs for Treatment\"* (December 2018), and represents a clinically meaningful population at risk for progression to cirrhosis and liver-related morbidity and mortality.

The Division agrees that subjects with cirrhosis (stage F4 fibrosis) should be excluded from this Phase 2b study, as proposed in the briefing package. The inclusion of subjects with cirrhosis would introduce significant heterogeneity in baseline disease severity and safety risk profile, and the Division considers it appropriate to evaluate PTX-4820 in a noncirrhotic NASH population before considering expansion to cirrhotic patients.

The Division does not raise concerns about the proposed age range of 18 to 75 years, which is consistent with enrollment criteria used in other NASH clinical development programs. The Division notes that the Sponsor should ensure that the study population is representative of the broader NASH patient population with respect to age, sex, race, and ethnicity, consistent with the FDA Guidance for Industry: *\"Enhancing the Diversity of Clinical Trial Populations --- Eligibility Criteria, Enrollment Practices, and Trial Designs\"* (November 2020).

The Division notes that the proposed alcohol consumption exclusion thresholds (greater than 30 grams per day for men and greater than 20 grams per day for women) are appropriate and consistent with accepted clinical definitions for distinguishing NASH from alcohol-associated steatohepatitis. The Division recommends that alcohol consumption be assessed using a validated instrument (e.g., the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test \[AUDIT\] or the timeline follow-back method) and that the assessment period cover at least the 12 months prior to screening.

The Division recommends that the Sponsor include an exclusion criterion for subjects with a Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score of 15 or greater at screening. Although the Sponsor\'s briefing package proposes to exclude subjects with \"hepatic decompensation,\" the Division notes that the term \"hepatic decompensation\" without a specific, objective, quantifiable definition may be subject to inconsistent interpretation across clinical sites. The MELD score provides an objective, quantifiable threshold for identifying subjects at higher risk of hepatic decompensation who may not be appropriate for participation in this trial. A MELD score of 15 or greater has been validated as a predictor of increased short-term mortality in patients with chronic liver disease and is widely used as a clinical benchmark. The Division considers a MELD score cutoff of 15 or greater to be an important safety measure for this study population and recommends that it be included as a specific, numeric exclusion criterion in the protocol, in addition to any clinical criteria for hepatic decompensation.

The Division further notes that the protocol should specify baseline liver biopsy adequacy criteria (as discussed in Section 4.1 above) and should define the required washout periods for any concomitant hepatotoxic medications, including but not limited to amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, and high-dose acetaminophen. The protocol should also specify which concomitant medications for metabolic comorbidities (e.g., statins, antidiabetic agents, antihypertensives) are permitted and whether stable dosing requirements apply.

**[4.4 Question 4 --- Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB)]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division recommend the establishment of an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) for this study?\"

**FDA Response.** The Division states that a Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) is expected for this trial. The Division wishes to be clear and unequivocal on this point: the establishment of an independent DSMB is not optional for this study. The Division emphasizes several factors that, in combination, make a DSMB essential rather than merely advisable:

> \(a\) **Invasive Procedures.** The study requires paired liver biopsies at baseline and Week 52. Percutaneous liver biopsy is an invasive procedure that carries inherent procedural risks, including but not limited to bleeding, infection, pneumothorax, and organ perforation. The procedural risk of liver biopsy necessitates ongoing, independent safety oversight to ensure that the benefits of study participation continue to outweigh the risks for enrolled subjects.
>
> \(b\) **Treatment Duration.** The 52-week treatment duration necessitates sustained safety surveillance over an extended period. Safety signals may emerge gradually over the course of a year of treatment that would not be apparent in shorter-duration studies, and an independent body is needed to conduct prospective, unblinded safety reviews at regular intervals.
>
> \(c\) **Study Population.** The study population consists of patients with advanced liver disease (stage F2 or F3 fibrosis) who are at elevated baseline risk of hepatic decompensation, progression to cirrhosis, and liver-related mortality. These patients represent a vulnerable population in whom emerging hepatotoxic signals from the investigational agent could have serious and potentially life-threatening consequences.
>
> \(d\) Novel Compound. PTX-4820 is a novel compound with limited human safety data. Although the GLP-1 receptor agonist class has an established safety profile in the context of diabetes and obesity, the dual GLP-1/GVP agonist mechanism in a NASH population with advanced fibrosis represents a first-in-class application in which the safety profile is not yet well characterized. The potential for hepatotoxicity, exacerbation of liver disease, or other serious adverse effects in this population has not been established.

The Division recommends that the DSMB for this study meet the following requirements:

> \(i\) The DSMB should be composed of independent experts who have no financial, employment, consultancy, or significant academic collaboration conflicts with the Sponsor. The DSMB should include, at a minimum, one board-certified hepatologist with clinical trial experience in NASH, one independent biostatistician with experience in interim data analysis and adaptive trial designs, and one clinical pharmacologist with expertise in GLP-1-based therapeutics or metabolic liver disease.
>
> \(ii\) The DSMB should operate under a written charter that is finalized

The charter should prespecify the schedule for regular safety reviews, the types of data to which the DSMB will have access (including unblinded safety data by treatment arm), the decision criteria and voting procedures for DSMB recommendations, and the communication procedures between the DSMB and the Sponsor.
>
> \(iii\) The DSMB should conduct scheduled safety reviews at defined intervals, including but not limited to: (1) after enrollment and dosing of the first 90 subjects (i.e., approximately 25% of planned enrollment); (2) at the time of any planned interim analysis; (3) at the time any predefined safety signals emerge; and (4) at any other time the DSMB determines a review is warranted based on accumulating data.
>
> \(iv\) The DSMB should have the authority to recommend study modifications (including dose modifications or changes to the dose-titration schedule), termination of one or more treatment arms, temporary suspension of enrollment, or discontinuation of the entire study. The Sponsor should commit in the protocol to giving serious and good-faith consideration to any DSMB recommendation, and the protocol should describe the process for implementing DSMB recommendations in a timely manner.

The Division emphasizes that the language in the protocol should make establishment of the DSMB mandatory, not discretionary. The protocol should state that a DSMB will be established and operational prior to enrollment of the first subject, and the DSMB charter should be included as an appendix to the IND application or submitted as a protocol amendment prior to study initiation. The Division would consider the absence of a DSMB commitment in the IND submission to be a significant deficiency that could contribute to a clinical hold determination under 21 CFR § 312.42.

**[4.5 Question 5 --- Stopping Rules and Safety Monitoring]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division have recommendations regarding stopping rules and predefined safety criteria for this study?\"

**FDA Response.** The Division has reviewed the Sponsor\'s proposed safety monitoring framework as described in the meeting briefing package. The Division notes that the Sponsor\'s briefing package included individual subject stopping rules for the following events:

> • Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevation greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal (ULN)
>
> • Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) meeting Hy\'s Law criteria (ALT or AST \>3× ULN concurrent with total bilirubin \>2× ULN in the absence of biliary obstruction)
>
> • Anaphylaxis or severe hypersensitivity reaction to PTX-4820

The Division considers these individual subject stopping rules to be generally appropriate and consistent with standard clinical practice for early-phase studies of compounds administered to patients with underlying liver disease. The Division notes that the ALT threshold of 10× ULN is appropriate given that subjects with NASH may have elevated baseline transaminase levels, and a lower threshold (e.g., 3× ULN or 5× ULN) could result in unnecessary study discontinuations in this population. The Division recommends that the protocol also include criteria for dose interruption and re-challenge at lower ALT thresholds (e.g., ALT \>5× ULN), with clear guidelines for when permanent discontinuation versus dose modification is appropriate.

However, the Division recommends that the protocol also include study-level stopping criteria that are distinct from, and operate independently of, the individual subject stopping rules described above. Study-level stopping criteria serve to protect the overall study population from emerging safety signals that may not be apparent at the individual subject level but become evident when data are aggregated across subjects within a treatment arm or across treatment arms.

Specifically, the Division recommends that the following hepatic decompensation events be included as predefined study-level stopping criteria that would trigger an expedited DSMB review and potential study-wide action:

> • Variceal bleeding
>
> • New-onset ascites or clinically significant worsening of pre-existing ascites
>
> • Hepatic encephalopathy (any grade)
>
> • Hepatorenal syndrome

The Division recommends that the protocol prespecify the number or rate of such hepatic decompensation events that would trigger mandatory DSMB review with the authority to recommend dose modification, arm discontinuation, or study termination. For example, the Division considers it appropriate for the protocol to specify that the occurrence of 2 or more hepatic decompensation events (as defined above) in any single treatment arm, or a statistically significant imbalance in the rate of hepatic decompensation events between any active treatment arm and the placebo arm, would trigger an expedited, unscheduled DSMB review. The specific thresholds should be developed by the Sponsor in consultation with the DSMB and prespecified in both the protocol and the DSMB charter prior to enrollment of the first subject.

The Division notes that study-level stopping criteria are conceptually and operationally distinct from individual subject stopping rules. Individual subject stopping rules govern the decision to discontinue study drug in a single participant based on that participant\'s clinical or laboratory data. Study-level stopping criteria, by contrast, govern the decision to modify, suspend, or terminate a treatment arm or the entire study based on the aggregate safety experience across subjects. Both types of criteria are important components of a comprehensive safety monitoring framework, and both should be prespecified in the protocol.

The Division also recommends enhanced liver safety monitoring consistent with the FDA Guidance for Industry: *\"Drug-Induced Liver Injury: Premarketing Clinical Evaluation\"* (July 2009). This should include frequent monitoring of hepatic function tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, total and direct bilirubin, albumin, and INR) at regular intervals throughout the study, with increased monitoring frequency during the initial titration period and following any dose escalation. The Division recommends that hepatic function tests be performed at least every 2 weeks during the first 12 weeks of treatment and at least monthly thereafter, with additional unscheduled assessments performed whenever clinically indicated.

**[4.6 Question 6 --- Interim Analysis]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division agree with the Sponsor\'s proposed interim analysis plan? The Sponsor proposes an interim efficacy analysis at Week 26 of the last enrolled subject, using an O\'Brien-Fleming alpha spending function.\"

**FDA Response.** The Division has reviewed the Sponsor\'s proposed interim analysis plan as described in the meeting briefing package and has two specific recommendations regarding the interim analysis approach.

**(a) Timing of the Interim Analysis.** The Division recommends that the interim analysis be conducted at the 50% enrollment mark --- that is, when approximately 180 subjects have been randomized and have had sufficient follow-up to contribute evaluable efficacy data --- rather than at Week 26 of the last enrolled subject, as proposed by the Sponsor. The Division notes that an analysis timed to Week 26 of the last enrolled subject would, by definition, occur very late in the overall study timeline. Given the anticipated 12-month enrollment period (October 2025 through October 2026) and the 52-week treatment duration, an analysis at Week 26 of the last enrolled subject would not occur until approximately April 2027 --- at which point the majority of subjects enrolled earlier in the study would have already completed the full 52-week treatment period. This timing would substantially reduce the practical utility of the interim analysis for informing early study decisions, including dose selection, sample size re-estimation, and early termination for futility.

An interim analysis conducted at the 50% enrollment mark --- approximately when 180 subjects have been randomized --- would allow for more timely decision-making while still providing a meaningful quantity of data for analysis. The Division acknowledges that at the 50% enrollment mark, not all of these subjects will have completed the full 52-week treatment period; therefore, the interim analysis may need to rely on early efficacy signals from surrogate or intermediate endpoints (e.g., noninvasive biomarker changes, liver enzyme improvements) in addition to any available histological data. The statistical analysis plan should prespecify the endpoints and data to be analyzed at the interim, the information fraction, and the decision rules.

**(b) Interim Futility Analysis.** The Division requests that the protocol include a formal interim futility analysis at the 50% enrollment mark, in addition to any planned interim efficacy analysis. The futility analysis should be prespecified in the statistical analysis plan with clearly defined futility boundaries and decision rules. The Division considers this to be an important component of the study design for the following reasons:

> Given the study size (360 subjects), the 52-week treatment duration, the cost and invasiveness of paired liver biopsies, and the known risks of the study procedures and investigational agent, an interim futility assessment is critically important to avoid exposing subjects to an ineffective treatment for the full study duration when early data indicate a low probability of achieving the primary endpoint. The principle of minimizing subject exposure to futile treatment is a core ethical consideration in clinical trial design.

The futility analysis should assess whether the conditional power for the primary endpoint (≥1-stage improvement in fibrosis with no worsening of NASH) has fallen below a prespecified threshold. The Division considers 20% conditional power, calculated based on the observed treatment effect at the time of the interim analysis, to be a reasonable threshold for declaring futility. If conditional power falls below this threshold for all active treatment arms, the DSMB should be empowered to recommend study termination for futility. If conditional power falls below the threshold for one or more individual treatment arms but not all, the DSMB should be empowered to recommend discontinuation of the affected arm(s) while the remaining arms continue.

The Division agrees that the O\'Brien-Fleming alpha spending function is an acceptable and well-established approach for controlling the overall Type I error rate at the interim efficacy analysis. The choice of the O\'Brien-Fleming boundary is conservative at early information fractions and closely preserves the final-analysis alpha level, which the Division considers appropriate for a Phase 2b study.

The Division recommends that the interim analysis (both efficacy and futility components) be conducted by an independent statistician who is not otherwise involved in the day-to-day conduct of the study and who operates under a firewall agreement to prevent dissemination of unblinded results to the Sponsor\'s study team. The results of the interim analysis should be reviewed by the DSMB, and the DSMB should communicate its recommendations to the Sponsor through a predefined communication pathway specified in the DSMB charter. The Sponsor\'s protocol team and study operations personnel should remain blinded to the interim analysis results unless the DSMB recommends unblinding or study termination.

The Division notes that all interim analysis procedures, including the timing, endpoints, statistical methods, decision rules, futility boundaries, and communication pathways, should be fully prespecified in the statistical analysis plan and the DSMB charter prior to enrollment of the first subject and should not be modified after enrollment begins without prospective notification to the Division.

**[4.7 Question 7 --- Nonclinical Package and IND Submission Timing]{.underline}**

**Sponsor\'s Question.** \"Does the Division consider the completed nonclinical package, including the 26-week GLP toxicology studies in rats and monkeys, to be adequate to support IND submission and initiation of a 52-week Phase 2b study?\"

**FDA Response.** The Division notes that a 26-week repeat-dose toxicology study duration in two species (one rodent and one non-rodent) is generally adequate to support a clinical study of up to 6 months in duration under the International Council for Harmonisation guidance ICH M3(R2): *\"Nonclinical Safety Studies for the Conduct of Human Clinical Trials and Marketing Authorization of Pharmaceuticals\"* (June 2009, as updated). The completed 26-week GLP toxicology studies in Sprague-Dawley rats and cynomolgus monkeys, as described in the Sponsor\'s briefing package, provide an acceptable nonclinical foundation for the initial IND submission.

However, for a proposed clinical treatment duration of 52 weeks (12 months), 9-month (39-week) chronic toxicology studies in non-rodent species would typically be expected under ICH M3(R2), Section 5. The Division acknowledges that the Sponsor may initiate the clinical study while the chronic toxicology studies are ongoing, provided that the following conditions are met: (1) the 26-week toxicology data in both species are adequate and do not reveal findings that would preclude clinical dosing; (2) the chronic (39-week) non-rodent toxicology study is initiated prior to or concurrent with the start of clinical dosing; and (3) the results of the chronic toxicology study are available before any study subject is dosed beyond 26 weeks of treatment. The Sponsor should provide a clear commitment and projected timeline for the completion and submission of the chronic toxicology data in the IND cover letter.

The Division recommends that the Sponsor submit the complete 26-week toxicology study reports (for both species) as part of the IND application, along with a tabulated summary of key findings, dose-response relationships, target organ toxicities, reversibility data, and the established no-observed-adverse-effect levels (NOAELs) and their safety margins relative to the proposed clinical doses. The Sponsor should also include the results of any genotoxicity studies (standard battery), safety pharmacology studies (core battery under ICH S7A and S7B), and reproductive toxicology studies that have been completed as of the IND submission date.

The Division notes that the Sponsor\'s target IND submission date of September 15, 2025, with an estimated first-subject-enrolled date of October 2025, is feasible provided the IND application is complete and does not raise any clinical hold issues under 21 CFR § 312.42. The Division\'s standard review period for an original IND application is 30 calendar days from receipt, during which the Division will determine whether the IND may proceed or whether a clinical hold is warranted.

The Division does not raise any specific concerns at this time regarding the compound\'s mechanism of action or the dual GLP-1/GVP pharmacology from a nonclinical perspective. However, the Division notes that this pre-IND meeting is based on the limited information provided in the briefing package, and the Division reserves the right to request additional nonclinical studies or data based on the full review of the IND application. In particular, the Division may request additional characterization of the following, depending on the data submitted: (a) thyroid C-cell effects, which are a known class effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists in rodents; (b) pancreatic safety, including assessment of pancreatitis and pancreatic proliferative lesions; and (c) cardiovascular safety, including QT/QTc assessment. The Sponsor should be prepared to address these topics in the IND application.

**[Section 5: Additional FDA Comments]{.underline}**

In addition to the responses to the Sponsor\'s specific questions set forth in Section 4, the Division provides the following additional comments on topics not raised in the Sponsor\'s questions but considered relevant to the proposed study design and IND submission.

**Statistical Design Considerations.** The Division notes that the Sponsor\'s proposed sample size of 360 subjects (90 per arm) and the underlying statistical assumptions --- including 80% power, a 15-percentage-point treatment difference (45% response rate in the high-dose arm versus 30% in the placebo arm), a two-sided alpha of 0.05 (adjusted for multiplicity), and a 15% allowance for dropout and non-evaluable subjects --- are generally reasonable for a Phase 2b dose-ranging study. The Division recommends that the Sponsor consider prespecifying an estimand framework consistent with the ICH E9(R1) Addendum: *\"Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis in Clinical Trials\"* (November 2019). The estimand framework should clearly define the treatment effect of interest, the population of interest, the variable (endpoint) of interest, the population-level summary measure, and the strategies for handling intercurrent events (e.g., treatment discontinuation, use of rescue medication, initiation of concomitant NASH therapies). The Division considers the estimand framework to be an important element of the statistical analysis plan and encourages the Sponsor to discuss its estimand strategy with the Office of Biostatistics.

**Key Secondary Endpoints.** The Division agrees that the following secondary endpoints, as proposed in the briefing package, are appropriate and clinically meaningful for a Phase 2b study in NASH with liver fibrosis: (a) NASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at Week 52; (b) ≥2-point reduction in NAFLD Activity Score (NAS) at Week 52; (c) change from baseline in serum ALT and AST at Week 52; (d) change from baseline in liver stiffness as measured by vibration-controlled transient elastography (FibroScan) at Weeks 26 and 52; (e) change from baseline in body weight at Weeks 26 and 52; and (f) pharmacokinetic parameters of PTX-4820 at steady state. The Division recommends that the multiplicity adjustment strategy for secondary endpoints be prespecified in the statistical analysis plan, including the hierarchical testing order if a fixed-sequence testing procedure is used.

**Multi-Site Coordination.** The Division notes that the Sponsor proposes to conduct the study at 28 clinical sites across the United States (22 sites) and Canada (6 sites). The Division reminds the Sponsor that all site investigators must be qualified by training and experience to conduct the study, and that investigator oversight and monitoring should be consistent with the requirements of ICH E6(R2): *\"Guideline for Good Clinical Practice\"* (November 2016, as amended). The Sponsor should ensure that site selection and qualification procedures are documented and that risk-based monitoring strategies are employed to maintain data integrity across a geographically distributed study.

**Electronic Data Capture.** The Division notes that all electronic data collection systems used in the trial should comply with applicable regulatory requirements for electronic records and electronic signatures, including 21 CFR Part 11. The Sponsor should ensure that the electronic data capture (EDC) system is validated and that audit trails are maintained for all data entries and modifications.

**Biomarker and Exploratory Endpoints.** The Division encourages the Sponsor to consider incorporating noninvasive biomarkers as exploratory endpoints to support future regulatory discussions regarding surrogate endpoints and to contribute to the broader understanding of treatment effects in NASH. Potential noninvasive biomarkers of interest include, but are not limited to: the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) score, Pro-C3 (a marker of type III collagen formation), cytokeratin-18 (CK-18) fragments (as a marker of hepatocyte apoptosis), the FibroTest/FibroSure panel, and magnetic resonance imaging-derived proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) for assessment of hepatic steatosis. The Division notes that while these biomarkers are not currently accepted as primary efficacy endpoints, their inclusion as exploratory endpoints would provide valuable data for the ongoing qualification of noninvasive biomarkers in NASH clinical trials and may be useful in supporting future regulatory submissions.

**[Section 6: Agreed-Upon Action Items]{.underline}**

The following action items were agreed upon by both parties during the meeting. These action items summarize the key commitments and next steps resulting from the discussions documented in these minutes.

1\. **Pinnacle Therapeutics** will revise the Phase 2b protocol (PTX-4820-201) to incorporate the Division\'s recommendations regarding the following elements:

> \(a\) **Centralized Pathology Review:** Implementation of a centralized pathology reading panel consisting of at least two independent hepatopathologists for scoring of all biopsy specimens, with adjudication by a third independent hepatopathologist in cases of disagreement, including prespecification of blinding procedures, disagreement criteria, adjudication process, and pathologist qualification and calibration requirements (see Section 4.1).
>
> \(b\) **Dose Titration for 30 mg Arm:** Revision of the dose-titration schedule for the 30 mg dose arm (Arm C) to include a minimum 4-week titration period, replacing the Sponsor\'s previously proposed 2-week titration schedule (see Section 4.2).
>
> \(c\) **MELD Score Exclusion Criterion:** Addition of a specific exclusion criterion excluding subjects with a Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score of 15 or greater at screening (see Section 4.3).
>
> \(d\) **Mandatory DSMB Establishment:** Revision of the protocol to include mandatory establishment of an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) with a written charter, prespecified review schedules, and defined authority to recommend study modifications or termination. The protocol language should make the DSMB mandatory, not discretionary (see Section 4.4).
>
> \(e\) **Study-Level Stopping Criteria:** Incorporation of predefined study-level stopping criteria for hepatic decompensation events (variceal bleeding, new-onset or worsening ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and hepatorenal syndrome), with prespecified thresholds for triggering mandatory expedited DSMB review (see Section 4.5).
>
> \(f\) **Interim Futility Analysis:** Revision of the interim analysis plan to (i) conduct the interim analysis at the 50% enrollment mark rather than at Week 26 of the last enrolled subject, and (ii) include a formal futility analysis with prespecified futility boundaries (20% conditional power threshold) and decision rules (see Section 4.6).

2\. **Pinnacle Therapeutics** will submit the revised protocol as part of the IND application for PTX-4820, targeted for submission on or before September 15, 2025.

3\. **Pinnacle Therapeutics** will provide a clear commitment and projected timeline for completion and submission of 9-month (39-week) chronic toxicology studies in the non-rodent species in the IND cover letter, with a commitment to submit the chronic toxicology data as an IND amendment before any study subject is dosed beyond 26 weeks of treatment.

4\. **Pinnacle Therapeutics** will prespecify biopsy adequacy criteria in the protocol, including minimum biopsy length of 1.5 cm and minimum of 6 portal tracts, and will describe procedures for handling inadequate biopsy specimens.

5\. **FDA (Division of Hepatology and Nutrition)** will review the IND application upon receipt and will communicate any deficiencies, including any clinical hold issues, within 30 calendar days of receipt of a complete IND submission pursuant to 21 CFR § 312.42.

6\. **Pinnacle Therapeutics** is encouraged to request a follow-up Type C meeting with the Division if additional questions arise during protocol finalization, statistical analysis plan development, or preparation of the IND application. The Division notes that a Type C meeting request may be submitted at any time and will be scheduled consistent with PDUFA goal dates for Type C meetings.

**[SECTION 2: INTRODUCTION AND REGULATORY FRAMEWORK]{.underline}**

**[2.1 Background and Rationale]{.underline}**

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a progressive form of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) characterized by hepatic steatosis accompanied by lobular inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning with or without fibrosis. NASH represents a significant and growing public health concern globally, with an estimated prevalence of 3--5% of the general adult population in developed countries. Among individuals with NAFLD, approximately 20--30% are estimated to have NASH. The prevalence of NASH is rising in parallel with the increasing prevalence of obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and metabolic syndrome, conditions that are closely linked to the development and progression of NASH.

The clinical significance of NASH lies in its potential for progressive liver fibrosis. Among patients with NASH, approximately 40% will develop progressive fibrosis over a follow-up period of 5--10 years, and a meaningful proportion will progress to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and need for liver transplantation. NASH is currently the second leading cause of liver transplantation in the United States and is projected to become the leading indication within the next decade. Importantly, liver fibrosis stage has been identified as the strongest independent predictor of liver-related morbidity and mortality in patients with NAFLD/NASH, highlighting the critical importance of targeting fibrosis as a therapeutic endpoint.

Despite the substantial disease burden, there are currently no pharmacotherapies approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) specifically for the treatment of NASH with liver fibrosis, as of the date of this protocol. Current management is limited to lifestyle modifications (dietary changes, exercise, weight loss) and management of associated metabolic comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension. While weight loss of ≥10% of body weight has been associated with histological improvement in NASH and fibrosis, achieving and sustaining this degree of weight loss through lifestyle measures alone is exceedingly difficult for most patients. There is therefore a critical unmet medical need for effective pharmacological therapies that can improve liver fibrosis and NASH histology.

**Mechanism of Action of PTX-4820.** PTX-4820 is a novel dual agonist of the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor and the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor. PTX-4820 is a synthetic peptide designed for once-weekly subcutaneous administration. The dual receptor agonism of PTX-4820 is hypothesized to produce complementary and synergistic effects on multiple pathways relevant to the pathogenesis and progression of NASH, including: (a) reduction in hepatic de novo lipogenesis via improved insulin sensitivity and direct hepatic metabolic effects; (b) anti-inflammatory effects mediated through reduction of hepatic macrophage activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production; (c) direct anti-fibrotic signaling through modulation of hepatic stellate cell activation and collagen deposition; and (d) weight loss through appetite suppression and enhanced satiety, providing indirect benefit to hepatic steatosis and inflammation.

**Preclinical Data.** The nonclinical development program for PTX-4820 included 26-week GLP (Good Laboratory Practice) toxicology studies in Sprague-Dawley rats and cynomolgus monkeys, completed in December 2024. These pivotal toxicology studies demonstrated a favorable safety profile across the dose ranges tested. In both species, PTX-4820 was well-tolerated at doses up to and including the highest dose tested, with the primary pharmacologic effects of reduced food consumption and body weight loss observed as expected for a GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist. Importantly, dose-dependent reductions in hepatic steatosis and fibrosis markers were observed in the rat model of diet-induced NASH (the STAM model), including significant reductions in liver triglyceride content, NAS components, and collagen proportionate area at the mid and high doses. No evidence of thyroid C-cell hyperplasia or neoplasia was observed in the 26-week rat study, although longer-duration carcinogenicity studies have not yet been completed. A comprehensive summary of the nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology data is provided in the Investigator\'s Brochure.

**Orphan Drug Designation.** The U.S. FDA granted Orphan Drug Designation to PTX-4820 for the treatment of NASH with liver fibrosis on November 8, 2024 (Designation #24-5773). This designation was based on the prevalence of the target population and the absence of approved therapies.

**Pinnacle Therapeutics Clinical Experience.** Pinnacle Therapeutics has prior clinical development experience with the incretin receptor agonist class through its lead program with PTX-3100, a selective GLP-1 receptor agonist currently in Phase 1 clinical evaluation for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus under IND 152847. The clinical and regulatory experience gained through the PTX-3100 program has informed the design of the PTX-4820 development program.

**Regulatory Interactions.** A Pre-IND Meeting (Type B meeting) was held with the FDA\'s Division of Hepatology and Nutrition (DHN) on March 12, 2025. Written minutes were received on April 2, 2025. The FDA provided guidance on the proposed Phase 2b study design, endpoints, safety monitoring approach, and general clinical development strategy for PTX-4820 in NASH. The recommendations from this meeting have been incorporated into the study design where appropriate, and the meeting minutes are maintained in the regulatory files.

**Clinical Rationale for Phase 2b Dose-Ranging Study.** Given the compelling preclinical efficacy signals, the favorable safety profile established in toxicology studies, and the mechanism of action supporting multiple complementary pathways in NASH pathogenesis, a Phase 2b dose-ranging study is warranted to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of PTX-4820 at three dose levels in adults with histologically confirmed NASH and liver fibrosis (stage F2 or F3). The dose range of 5 mg to 30 mg weekly was selected based on pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling informed by preclinical data and early clinical experience with PTX-3100. This study is designed to identify the optimal dose or doses for advancement into Phase 3 pivotal trials.

This study will be conducted under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application submitted to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), Division of Hepatology and Nutrition (DHN), within the Office of Immunology and Inflammation. The IND application will include all required components, including the Investigator\'s Brochure, clinical protocol, informed consent form, chemistry and manufacturing controls information, and nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology data.

This study will be conducted in compliance with the following applicable U.S. regulations and guidelines:

>
> • **ICH E6(R2)** --- Guideline for Good Clinical Practice: the international ethical and scientific quality standard for the design, conduct, performance, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysis, and reporting of clinica
