H(2, "C. Safety Reporting")
FINDING("M-1", "Safety reporting framework does not track 21 CFR 312.32 or 312.64", "Major",
 "§9.1 (Sponsor will report “as required by applicable law”; investigator SAE reporting “within 48 hours”; AE collection begins at first dose; pre-dose events recorded as medical history; causality “related / not related”); §9.2 (AESIs within 48 hours)",
 "21 CFR 312.32(a), (c)(1)(i)–(iv), (c)(2), (d); 21 CFR 312.64(b); FDA Guidance, Safety Reporting Requirements for INDs and BA/BE Studies (Dec. 2012); ICH E6(R2) 4.11, 5.16–5.17; ICH E2A",
 "Section 9.1 states only that the Sponsor will report “as required by applicable law.” Specifically, the Protocol: (i) does not define “suspected adverse reaction,” “unexpected,” or “serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction” (SUSAR) as §312.32(a) does; (ii) does not name the reference safety information against which expectedness is judged (the IB section); (iii) states neither the **15-calendar-day** IND safety report deadline (§312.32(c)(1)) nor the **7-calendar-day** deadline for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions (§312.32(c)(2)); (iv) omits the other §312.32(c)(1) report triggers, including findings from other studies, animal or in vitro testing, and a clinically important increase in the rate of serious suspected adverse reactions over the protocol or IB; (v) has no plan for aggregate unblinded safety review (2012 Guidance) and no description of how IND safety reports reach investigators and IRBs/REBs; and (vi) gives investigators 48 hours to report SAEs. Section 312.64(b) requires investigators to report any SAE to the sponsor “immediately,” and industry practice and ICH E6(R2) 4.11.1 treat that as within 24 hours. A further gap: AE and SAE collection starts at first dose, and earlier events are recorded as medical history. As a result, **SAEs caused by the protocol-mandated screening liver biopsy would not be captured as SAEs**. Note also that several items on the working checklist cite the pre-2011 numbering of §312.32 (e.g., placing the 7-day rule in (c)(1)(i) and animal findings in §312.32(d)). They should be corrected to the current rule.",
 "Safety reporting is a core IND obligation, and a protocol that defers entirely to “applicable law” tends to draw FDA comment. The 48-hour window departs from §312.64(b) for every investigator who signs a Form FDA 1572. Missing biopsy-related SAEs during screening is a subject-safety and data-integrity gap.",
 ["Restate §9.1 to include the definitions, timelines and reporting pathways (below). Name the IB section that serves as reference safety information.",
  "Change investigator SAE reporting to immediately, and in no event later than 24 hours after awareness. Keep 24 hours for AESIs and for pregnancy.",
  "Collect SAEs, and all AEs related to study procedures, from signature of the ICF. Collect all other AEs from first dose.",
  "Add a statement on unblinding for expedited reporting (already in §5.3), on aggregate safety review by a Safety Assessment Committee or the DSMB, and on parallel Health Canada ADR reporting (M-2)."],
 "9.1.x Expedited Reporting to Regulatory Authorities. The Sponsor will evaluate each SAE for causality and expectedness against the Reference Safety Information in Section [X] of the current Investigator’s Brochure. A suspected adverse reaction is any adverse event for which there is a reasonable possibility that the study drug caused the event. The Sponsor will submit an IND safety report to FDA, and notify all participating investigators, of any suspected adverse reaction that is both serious and unexpected, and of any finding described in 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(ii)–(iv), as soon as possible and in no event later than 15 calendar days after the Sponsor determines that the information qualifies for reporting. Any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction will be reported to FDA as soon as possible and in no event later than 7 calendar days after the Sponsor’s initial receipt of the information. Relevant follow-up information will be submitted as an IND safety report without delay, and no later than 15 calendar days after receipt. Investigators will promptly forward IND safety reports to their IRB/REB as required. For Canadian sites, serious unexpected adverse drug reactions will be reported to Health Canada as described in Section 13.7. Investigator reporting: the investigator must report every SAE to the Sponsor immediately, and in no event later than 24 hours after becoming aware of it. SAEs are collected from the time the subject signs the ICF through the Week 64 visit.")

H(2, "D. Subject Protection, Nonclinical Support and Safety Monitoring")
FINDING("M-4", "No gating of dosing beyond Week 26 on 39-week chronic toxicology", "Major",
 "§2.1 (26-week rat and monkey studies only); §5.2 (dosing through Week 52); §13.1",
 "Minutes §4.7 and Action Item 3; ICH M3(R2) §5 (duration of repeated-dose toxicity studies); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8); 312.42(b)(1)(iv)",
 "The 26-week studies support clinical dosing up to 6 months. FDA allowed the 52-week study to start only on three conditions: (1) acceptable 26-week data; (2) the 39-week non-rodent study starting before or with clinical dosing; and (3) **39-week results available before any subject is dosed beyond 26 weeks**. Pinnacle must commit to this, with a timeline, in the IND cover letter and must submit the data as an IND amendment. The Protocol does not mention the requirement or any operational gate. The first subject to reach Week 26 is expected around April 2026, so the 39-week study must be under way now and reported by then.",
 "If a subject is dosed past Week 26 without the chronic data, Pinnacle would be in breach of the condition FDA set and would create a hold rationale under §312.42(b)(1)(iv) (insufficient information to assess risk). The Protocol should make the gate visible to investigators and the IRT.",
 ["Add a §5.2 gate (below). Program the IRT to block dispensing of Week 27+ kits until the Sponsor releases the gate.",
  "Pinnacle Nonclinical to confirm that the 39-week cynomolgus study has started, give its reporting date, and draft the cover-letter commitment. Have a contingency (e.g., treatment interruption or a protocol amendment) if the report will be late."],
 "5.2.x Dosing Beyond Week 26. Dosing of any subject beyond 26 weeks of treatment is contingent on the Sponsor’s submission to FDA [and Health Canada] of the results of the 39-week repeat-dose toxicology study in cynomolgus monkeys, and on the absence of findings that preclude continued dosing. The Sponsor will notify investigators in writing and release Week 27+ study drug through the IRT only after this condition is met. If the condition is not met by the time a subject reaches Week 26, study drug will be [interrupted] and the subject will continue scheduled assessments pending the Sponsor’s notification.")

FINDING("M-5", "Hepatic laboratory monitoring less frequent than FDA recommended; incomplete interruption / re-challenge rules", "Major",
 "Table 4 / Appendix C (CMP at Wks 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, then 30, 36, 42, 48, 52; INR only at Day 1, Wks 12, 24, 52); §9.5.1",
 "Minutes §4.5; FDA Guidance, Drug-Induced Liver Injury: Premarketing Clinical Evaluation (July 2009); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(6)(iii)(g)",
 "FDA recommended hepatic function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, total and direct bilirubin, albumin and INR) **at least every 2 weeks during the first 12 weeks and at least monthly thereafter**, with more testing during titration. The schedule has no draws at Weeks 6 and 10, spaces draws 6 weeks apart from Week 24 to Week 52, and measures INR only four times. FDA also asked for dose-interruption and re-challenge criteria at lower ALT thresholds (e.g., >5× ULN). Section 9.5.1 provides a 5–10× ULN hold-and-resume rule. But it does not account for elevated baseline transaminases, which are common in NASH; the DILI Guidance supports thresholds relative to baseline for such subjects. It also has no close-observation rule for ALT >3× ULN with symptoms, and no criteria for when a re-challenge is not permitted.",
 "This is a departure from a specific FDA safety recommendation in a population FDA called vulnerable. It is moderate hold risk but highly likely to draw an information request.",
 ["Add laboratory-only visits (central lab via local draw or mobile phlebotomy) at Weeks 6 and 10. Add monthly hepatic panels and INR at Weeks 28, 32/34, 40 and 44 so that intervals never exceed 4 weeks. Include INR in every hepatic panel.",
  "Expand §9.5.1 with baseline-adjusted thresholds (e.g., ALT >3× baseline or >5× ULN, whichever is lower, for subjects with elevated baseline), close-observation requirements, a prohibition on re-challenge after Hy’s Law or symptomatic hepatitis, and Medical Monitor and DSMB notification. Align with the Sponsor DILI Assessment Protocol cited in §9.2."])

FINDING("M-6", "Biopsy adequacy criteria differ from the agreed criteria; no repeat-biopsy procedure", "Major",
 "§8.1 (minimum 20 mm and 11 portal tracts; investigator “should consider obtaining an additional specimen”); §6.3 and Table 4 footnote b (fresh baseline biopsy if screening biopsy >4 weeks before Day 1); Inclusion 2 and 6",
 "Minutes §4.1 and Action Item 4; FDA NASH Guidance (Dec. 2018)",
 "Pinnacle agreed to prespecify a minimum biopsy length of **1.5 cm** and **6 portal tracts**, and to describe how inadequate specimens are handled, including whether a repeat biopsy will be offered and **the timeframe** for obtaining it. Section 8.1 sets stricter thresholds (20 mm and 11 portal tracts) without explanation. That may disqualify specimens FDA would accept, including historical qualifying biopsies, and so increase repeat invasive procedures. The repeat-biopsy provision is discretionary and has no time window. Related inconsistencies: Inclusion 2 accepts a biopsy taken within 6 months, but Table 4 note b requires a fresh baseline biopsy if the qualifying biopsy is more than 4 weeks before Day 1. Some subjects will therefore undergo three biopsies, which the ICF does not disclose (M-9). And the adequacy criteria are not expressly applied to historical biopsies or to the Week 52 specimen.",
 "This departs from an agreed action item. Stricter-than-agreed thresholds are not unlawful, but they must be justified because they add subject risk (repeat biopsies) and missing primary-endpoint data. FDA will look for the agreed criteria and the repeat-biopsy procedure.",
 ["Adopt the FDA criteria (≥1.5 cm and ≥6 portal tracts) as the adequacy definition. If Pinnacle Clinical prefers a stricter “target” specimen quality, state it as a target and keep the FDA minimum as the adequacy threshold.",
  "Prespecify (below): who judges adequacy (central pathology), the repeat-biopsy offer, windows for Screening and Week 52, and how inadequate specimens are handled in the analysis (link to the estimand, M-8).",
  "Reconcile the 6-month and 4-week windows for historical biopsies. FDA did not require a fresh baseline biopsy within 4 weeks. If one is retained, explain the scientific rationale and disclose the possibility in the ICF."],
 "8.1.x Biopsy Adequacy. A specimen is adequate for NASH CRN scoring if it is at least 1.5 cm in length and contains at least 6 portal tracts, as determined by the central pathology laboratory. This criterion applies to historical qualifying biopsies, screening/baseline biopsies and Week 52 biopsies. If a screening/baseline specimen is inadequate, the subject may be offered one repeat biopsy within the Screening period (no later than [14] days before Day 1). If a Week 52 specimen is inadequate, the subject may be offered one repeat biopsy within [4] weeks after the Week 52 visit, during which study drug [will/will not] continue. Subjects will not be required to undergo more than [one] repeat biopsy per timepoint.")

H(2, "E. Statistical Design")
FINDING("M-7", "Sample-size calculation does not support the stated 80% power", "Major",
 "§10.1, Table 5 and Table 1 (78 evaluable per arm; “78 / 0.85 ≈ 92, rounded to 90”); §10.4 (Hochberg across three dose comparisons); §10.3 (interim alpha spending)",
 "ICH E9 §3.5 (sample size); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(6)(iii); 312.42(b)(2)(ii); Minutes §5 (assumptions “generally reasonable,” with alpha “adjusted for multiplicity”)",
 "FDA accepted the **assumptions** (30% placebo vs. 45% at 30 mg, 80% power, two-sided α 0.05 adjusted for multiplicity, 15% dropout). On our arithmetic, the **calculation** in §10.1 does not follow from them. With the standard normal-approximation formula for two proportions, 30% vs. 45% at two-sided α = 0.05 and 80% power needs about **163 evaluable subjects per arm** (about 175 with continuity correction), not 78. At 76.5 evaluable per arm (90 × 0.85), the power for the stated difference is about **48%**. In addition: (i) 78/0.85 is 91.8, which the Protocol rounds **down** to 90, below its own evaluable target; (ii) the calculation makes no allowance for the Hochberg procedure across three dose comparisons (§10.4) or for the alpha spent at the interim analysis (§10.3), although FDA understood the alpha would be “adjusted for multiplicity”; and (iii) §10.4 calls 30 mg vs. placebo “the primary comparison” while applying Hochberg to all three comparisons. Those two statements are inconsistent.",
 "A dose-ranging Phase 2b study need not be powered for every comparison. But a protocol that states 80% power when the design delivers roughly half that power is an inaccuracy in a required IND element (§312.23(a)(6)(iii)). It risks a “clearly deficient in design” comment under §312.42(b)(2)(ii) and erodes credibility on the statistical matters FDA discussed. Correcting it may change enrollment, the number of sites and the $67.4 million budget, so it needs an early decision.",
 ["Pinnacle Biostatistics (Dr. Lattimore) to re-run and document the calculation, including software, test (CMH vs. chi-square), multiplicity and interim adjustments. Then either (a) increase the sample size, (b) restate the objective and power claim (e.g., as dose-response estimation via MCP-Mod/Emax with an appropriate power statement), or (c) revise the assumptions with a cited justification.",
  "Reconcile the primary-comparison language with the Hochberg family, and integrate the key secondary hierarchy (§10.5) into one prespecified multiplicity strategy (e.g., a graphical approach), as FDA requested (Minutes §5).",
  "If the sample size changes materially, consider informing the Division before submission (Type C meeting or written request)."])

FINDING("M-8", "No estimand framework; analysis populations depend on completion", "Major",
 "§10.2 (ITT = randomized and dosed; mITT, the primary population, requires a Week 52 biopsy); §10.4 (MAR multiple imputation as sensitivity analysis); §2.2 (cites ICH E9(R1))",
 "ICH E9(R1) Addendum (Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis), as adopted by FDA (May 2021); Minutes §5; FDA NASH Guidance (Dec. 2018)",
 "FDA recommended an estimand framework defining the treatment, population, variable, population-level summary and the strategies for intercurrent events (treatment discontinuation, rescue medication, starting other NASH therapy). The Protocol cites E9(R1) in §2.2 but has no estimand. The primary analysis population (mITT) includes only subjects with a Week 52 biopsy. It is therefore effectively a completers analysis, which can be biased if dropout differs between arms. FDA warned about exactly that differential dropout in the 30 mg arm (Minutes §4.2). The “ITT” label applies to dosed subjects only, not all randomized subjects. Handling missing biopsies under a missing-at-random assumption is not the conservative approach often used for NASH histology responder endpoints, where subjects without a biopsy are typically counted as non-responders.",
 "FDA can be expected to raise this at IND review and again at end-of-Phase 2. Phase 3 planning will rest on these estimates.",
 ["Add a §10.x Estimands section defining the primary estimand and its intercurrent-event strategies (e.g., composite strategy: discontinuation for lack of efficacy or AE, or missing Week 52 biopsy, counted as non-response; treatment-policy strategy for permitted background-medication changes). Define ITT as all randomized subjects. Align sensitivity analyses (tipping point and MNAR) with the estimand.",
  "Prespecify how inadequate biopsies (M-6) and initiation of prohibited NASH therapies such as resmetirom (M-11) are handled."])

H(2, "F. Data Integrity and Electronic Systems")
FINDING("M-3", "No 21 CFR Part 11 provisions for the TrialVault EDC system", "Major",
 "§12.1 (TrialVault described; role-based access, unique login and password, edit checks; no reference to Part 11, validation, audit trail, electronic signatures, backup/recovery)",
 "21 CFR Part 11 (§§11.10(a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (g), (k); 11.50; 11.70; 11.100–11.300); ICH E6(R2) 5.5.3; FDA Guidance, Use of Electronic Records and Electronic Signatures in Clinical Investigations Under 21 CFR Part 11 — Questions and Answers (Oct. 2024 final); Minutes §5 (“Electronic Data Capture”)",
 "FDA reminded Pinnacle that EDC systems must comply with Part 11, be validated, and keep audit trails. Section 12.1 does not mention Part 11. It also does not address other computerized systems that generate trial records: the IRT (Meridian), central laboratory (Greystone), central pathology, ePRO/injection diaries if electronic, and FibroScan data transfer. The working checklist items 312-035 and GCP-012 remain unassessed.",
 "Part 11 gaps are a frequent BIMO inspection finding. They can render electronic records unreliable for submission. They are unlikely to cause a hold, but they are a material data-integrity risk.",
 ["Add Part 11 language to §12.1 (below). Obtain from Trident the TrialVault validation summary, audit-trail specification and Part 11 assessment before first enrollment. Confirm Pinnacle’s §11.100(c) e-signature certification letter is on file with FDA.",
  "Extend vendor qualification and Part 11 assessments to the IRT, central lab and pathology systems."],
 "12.1.x Electronic Records and Signatures. TrialVault and all other computerized systems used to create, modify, maintain, archive, retrieve or transmit study records (including the IRT, central laboratory and central pathology systems) will comply with 21 CFR Part 11 and ICH E6(R2) Section 5.5.3. Before first data entry, Trident CRO will document validation of TrialVault for its intended use. Access is restricted to authorized individuals through unique credentials and role-based permissions, with a current list of individuals authorized to make data changes. Electronic signatures are unique to each individual, linked to their records, and executed in accordance with 21 CFR 11.50, 11.70 and 11.100–11.300. Data will be backed up at least [daily] with documented, tested recovery procedures. EDC configuration will preserve the blind.")

FINDING("M-1", "Safety reporting framework does not track 21 CFR 312.32 or 312.64", "Major",
 "§9.1 (Sponsor will report “as required by applicable law”; investigator SAE reporting “within 48 hours”; AE collection begins at first dose; pre-dose events recorded as medical history; causality “related / not related”); §9.2 (AESIs within 48 hours)",
 "21 CFR 312.32(a), (c)(1)(i)–(iv), (c)(2), (d); 21 CFR 312.64(b); FDA Guidance, Safety Reporting Requirements for INDs and BA/BE Studies (Dec. 2012); ICH E6(R2) 4.11, 5.16–5.17; ICH E2A",
 "Section 9.1 states only that the Sponsor will report “as required by applicable law.” Specifically, the Protocol: (i) does not define “suspected adverse reaction,” “unexpected,” or “serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction” (SUSAR) as §312.32(a) does; (ii) does not name the reference safety information against which expectedness is judged (the IB section); (iii) states neither the **15-calendar-day** IND safety report deadline (§312.32(c)(1)) nor the **7-calendar-day** deadline for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions (§312.32(c)(2)); (iv) omits the other §312.32(c)(1) report triggers, including findings from other studies, animal or in vitro testing, and a clinically important increase in the rate of serious suspected adverse reactions over the protocol or IB; (v) has no plan for aggregate unblinded safety review (2012 Guidance) and no description of how IND safety reports reach investigators and IRBs/REBs; and (vi) gives investigators 48 hours to report SAEs. Section 312.64(b) requires investigators to report any SAE to the sponsor “immediately,” and industry practice and ICH E6(R2) 4.11.1 treat that as within 24 hours. A further gap: AE and SAE collection starts at first dose, and earlier events are recorded as medical history. As a result, **SAEs caused by the protocol-mandated screening liver biopsy would not be captured as SAEs**. Note also that several items on the working checklist cite the pre-2011 numbering of §312.32 (e.g., placing the 7-day rule in (c)(1)(i) and animal findings in §312.32(d)). They should be corrected to the current rule.",
 "Safety reporting is a core IND obligation, and a protocol that defers entirely to “applicable law” tends to draw FDA comment. The 48-hour window departs from §312.64(b) for every investigator who signs a Form FDA 1572. Missing biopsy-related SAEs during screening is a subject-safety and data-integrity gap.",
 ["Restate §9.1 to include the definitions, timelines and reporting pathways (below). Name the IB section that serves as reference safety information.",
  "Change investigator SAE reporting to immediately, and in no event later than 24 hours after awareness. Keep 24 hours for AESIs and for pregnancy.",
  "Collect SAEs, and all AEs related to study procedures, from signature of the ICF. Collect all other AEs from first dose.",
  "Add a statement on unblinding for expedited reporting (already in §5.3), on aggregate safety review by a Safety Assessment Committee or the DSMB, and on parallel Health Canada ADR reporting (M-2)."],
 "9.1.x Expedited Reporting to Regulatory Authorities. The Sponsor will evaluate each SAE for causality and expectedness against the Reference Safety Information in Section [X] of the current Investigator’s Brochure. A suspected adverse reaction is any adverse event for which there is a reasonable possibility that the study drug caused the event. The Sponsor will submit an IND safety report to FDA, and notify all participating investigators, of any suspected adverse reaction that is both serious and unexpected, and of any finding described in 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(ii)–(iv), as soon as possible and in no event later than 15 calendar days after the Sponsor determines that the information qualifies for reporting. Any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction will be reported to FDA as soon as possible and in no event later than 7 calendar days after the Sponsor’s initial receipt of the information. Relevant follow-up information will be submitted as an IND safety report without delay, and no later than 15 calendar days after receipt. Investigators will promptly forward IND safety reports to their IRB/REB as required. For Canadian sites, serious unexpected adverse drug reactions will be reported to Health Canada as described in Section 13.7. Investigator reporting: the investigator must report every SAE to the Sponsor immediately, and in no event later than 24 hours after becoming aware of it. SAEs are collected from the time the subject signs the ICF through the Week 64 visit.")

H(2, "D. Subject Protection, Nonclinical Support and Safety Monitoring")
FINDING("M-4", "No gating of dosing beyond Week 26 on 39-week chronic toxicology", "Major",
 "§2.1 (26-week rat and monkey studies only); §5.2 (dosing through Week 52); §13.1",
 "Minutes §4.7 and Action Item 3; ICH M3(R2) §5 (duration of repeated-dose toxicity studies); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8); 312.42(b)(1)(iv)",
 "The 26-week studies support clinical dosing up to 6 months. FDA allowed the 52-week study to start only on three conditions: (1) acceptable 26-week data; (2) the 39-week non-rodent study starting before or with clinical dosing; and (3) **39-week results available before any subject is dosed beyond 26 weeks**. Pinnacle must commit to this, with a timeline, in the IND cover letter and must submit the data as an IND amendment. The Protocol does not mention the requirement or any operational gate. The first subject to reach Week 26 is expected around April 2026, so the 39-week study must be under way now and reported by then.",
 "If a subject is dosed past Week 26 without the chronic data, Pinnacle would be in breach of the condition FDA set and would create a hold rationale under §312.42(b)(1)(iv) (insufficient information to assess risk). The Protocol should make the gate visible to investigators and the IRT.",
 ["Add a §5.2 gate (below). Program the IRT to block dispensing of Week 27+ kits until the Sponsor releases the gate.",
  "Pinnacle Nonclinical to confirm that the 39-week cynomolgus study has started, give its reporting date, and draft the cover-letter commitment. Have a contingency (e.g., treatment interruption or a protocol amendment) if the report will be late."],
 "5.2.x Dosing Beyond Week 26. Dosing of any subject beyond 26 weeks of treatment is contingent on the Sponsor’s submission to FDA [and Health Canada] of the results of the 39-week repeat-dose toxicology study in cynomolgus monkeys, and on the absence of findings that preclude continued dosing. The Sponsor will notify investigators in writing and release Week 27+ study drug through the IRT only after this condition is met. If the condition is not met by the time a subject reaches Week 26, study drug will be [interrupted] and the subject will continue scheduled assessments pending the Sponsor’s notification.")

FINDING("M-5", "Hepatic laboratory monitoring less frequent than FDA recommended; incomplete interruption / re-challenge rules", "Major",
 "Table 4 / Appendix C (CMP at Wks 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, then 30, 36, 42, 48, 52; INR only at Day 1, Wks 12, 24, 52); §9.5.1",
 "Minutes §4.5; FDA Guidance, Drug-Induced Liver Injury: Premarketing Clinical Evaluation (July 2009); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(6)(iii)(g)",
 "FDA recommended hepatic function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, total and direct bilirubin, albumin and INR) **at least every 2 weeks during the first 12 weeks and at least monthly thereafter**, with more testing during titration. The schedule has no draws at Weeks 6 and 10, spaces draws 6 weeks apart from Week 24 to Week 52, and measures INR only four times. FDA also asked for dose-interruption and re-challenge criteria at lower ALT thresholds (e.g., >5× ULN). Section 9.5.1 provides a 5–10× ULN hold-and-resume rule. But it does not account for elevated baseline transaminases, which are common in NASH; the DILI Guidance supports thresholds relative to baseline for such subjects. It also has no close-observation rule for ALT >3× ULN with symptoms, and no criteria for when a re-challenge is not permitted.",
 "This is a departure from a specific FDA safety recommendation in a population FDA called vulnerable. It is moderate hold risk but highly likely to draw an information request.",
 ["Add laboratory-only visits (central lab via local draw or mobile phlebotomy) at Weeks 6 and 10. Add monthly hepatic panels and INR at Weeks 28, 32/34, 40 and 44 so that intervals never exceed 4 weeks. Include INR in every hepatic panel.",
  "Expand §9.5.1 with baseline-adjusted thresholds (e.g., ALT >3× baseline or >5× ULN, whichever is lower, for subjects with elevated baseline), close-observation requirements, a prohibition on re-challenge after Hy’s Law or symptomatic hepatitis, and Medical Monitor and DSMB notification. Align with the Sponsor DILI Assessment Protocol cited in §9.2."])

FINDING("M-6", "Biopsy adequacy criteria differ from the agreed criteria; no repeat-biopsy procedure", "Major",
 "§8.1 (minimum 20 mm and 11 portal tracts; investigator “should consider obtaining an additional specimen”); §6.3 and Table 4 footnote b (fresh baseline biopsy if screening biopsy >4 weeks before Day 1); Inclusion 2 and 6",
 "Minutes §4.1 and Action Item 4; FDA NASH Guidance (Dec. 2018)",
 "Pinnacle agreed to prespecify a minimum biopsy length of **1.5 cm** and **6 portal tracts**, and to describe how inadequate specimens are handled, including whether a repeat biopsy will be offered and **the timeframe** for obtaining it. Section 8.1 sets stricter thresholds (20 mm and 11 portal tracts) without explanation. That may disqualify specimens FDA would accept, including historical qualifying biopsies, and so increase repeat invasive procedures. The repeat-biopsy provision is discretionary and has no time window. Related inconsistencies: Inclusion 2 accepts a biopsy taken within 6 months, but Table 4 note b requires a fresh baseline biopsy if the qualifying biopsy is more than 4 weeks before Day 1. Some subjects will therefore undergo three biopsies, which the ICF does not disclose (M-9). And the adequacy criteria are not expressly applied to historical biopsies or to the Week 52 specimen.",
 "This departs from an agreed action item. Stricter-than-agreed thresholds are not unlawful, but they must be justified because they add subject risk (repeat biopsies) and missing primary-endpoint data. FDA will look for the agreed criteria and the repeat-biopsy procedure.",
 ["Adopt the FDA criteria (≥1.5 cm and ≥6 portal tracts) as the adequacy definition. If Pinnacle Clinical prefers a stricter “target” specimen quality, state it as a target and keep the FDA minimum as the adequacy threshold.",
  "Prespecify (below): who judges adequacy (central pathology), the repeat-biopsy offer, windows for Screening and Week 52, and how inadequate specimens are handled in the analysis (link to the estimand, M-8).",
  "Reconcile the 6-month and 4-week windows for historical biopsies. FDA did not require a fresh baseline biopsy within 4 weeks. If one is retained, explain the scientific rationale and disclose the possibility in the ICF."],
 "8.1.x Biopsy Adequacy. A specimen is adequate for NASH CRN scoring if it is at least 1.5 cm in length and contains at least 6 portal tracts, as determined by the central pathology laboratory. This criterion applies to historical qualifying biopsies, screening/baseline biopsies and Week 52 biopsies. If a screening/baseline specimen is inadequate, the subject may be offered one repeat biopsy within the Screening period (no later than [14] days before Day 1). If a Week 52 specimen is inadequate, the subject may be offered one repeat biopsy within [4] weeks after the Week 52 visit, during which study drug [will/will not] continue. Subjects will not be required to undergo more than [one] repeat biopsy per timepoint.")

H(2, "E. Statistical Design")
FINDING("M-7", "Sample-size calculation does not support the stated 80% power", "Major",
 "§10.1, Table 5 and Table 1 (78 evaluable per arm; “78 / 0.85 ≈ 92, rounded to 90”); §10.4 (Hochberg across three dose comparisons); §10.3 (interim alpha spending)",
 "ICH E9 §3.5 (sample size); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(6)(iii); 312.42(b)(2)(ii); Minutes §5 (assumptions “generally reasonable,” with alpha “adjusted for multiplicity”)",
 "FDA accepted the **assumptions** (30% placebo vs. 45% at 30 mg, 80% power, two-sided α 0.05 adjusted for multiplicity, 15% dropout). On our arithmetic, the **calculation** in §10.1 does not follow from them. With the standard normal-approximation formula for two proportions, 30% vs. 45% at two-sided α = 0.05 and 80% power needs about **163 evaluable subjects per arm** (about 175 with continuity correction), not 78. At 76.5 evaluable per arm (90 × 0.85), the power for the stated difference is about **48%**. In addition: (i) 78/0.85 is 91.8, which the Protocol rounds **down** to 90, below its own evaluable target; (ii) the calculation makes no allowance for the Hochberg procedure across three dose comparisons (§10.4) or for the alpha spent at the interim analysis (§10.3), although FDA understood the alpha would be “adjusted for multiplicity”; and (iii) §10.4 calls 30 mg vs. placebo “the primary comparison” while applying Hochberg to all three comparisons. Those two statements are inconsistent.",
 "A dose-ranging Phase 2b study need not be powered for every comparison. But a protocol that states 80% power when the design delivers roughly half that power is an inaccuracy in a required IND element (§312.23(a)(6)(iii)). It risks a “clearly deficient in design” comment under §312.42(b)(2)(ii) and erodes credibility on the statistical matters FDA discussed. Correcting it may change enrollment, the number of sites and the $67.4 million budget, so it needs an early decision.",
 ["Pinnacle Biostatistics (Dr. Lattimore) to re-run and document the calculation, including software, test (CMH vs. chi-square), multiplicity and interim adjustments. Then either (a) increase the sample size, (b) restate the objective and power claim (e.g., as dose-response estimation via MCP-Mod/Emax with an appropriate power statement), or (c) revise the assumptions with a cited justification.",
  "Reconcile the primary-comparison language with the Hochberg family, and integrate the key secondary hierarchy (§10.5) into one prespecified multiplicity strategy (e.g., a graphical approach), as FDA requested (Minutes §5).",
  "If the sample size changes materially, consider informing the Division before submission (Type C meeting or written request)."])

FINDING("M-8", "No estimand framework; analysis populations depend on completion", "Major",
 "§10.2 (ITT = randomized and dosed; mITT, the primary population, requires a Week 52 biopsy); §10.4 (MAR multiple imputation as sensitivity analysis); §2.2 (cites ICH E9(R1))",
 "ICH E9(R1) Addendum (Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis), as adopted by FDA (May 2021); Minutes §5; FDA NASH Guidance (Dec. 2018)",
 "FDA recommended an estimand framework defining the treatment, population, variable, population-level summary and the strategies for intercurrent events (treatment discontinuation, rescue medication, starting other NASH therapy). The Protocol cites E9(R1) in §2.2 but has no estimand. The primary analysis population (mITT) includes only subjects with a Week 52 biopsy. It is therefore effectively a completers analysis, which can be biased if dropout differs between arms. FDA warned about exactly that differential dropout in the 30 mg arm (Minutes §4.2). The “ITT” label applies to dosed subjects only, not all randomized subjects. Handling missing biopsies under a missing-at-random assumption is not the conservative approach often used for NASH histology responder endpoints, where subjects without a biopsy are typically counted as non-responders.",
 "FDA can be expected to raise this at IND review and again at end-of-Phase 2. Phase 3 planning will rest on these estimates.",
 ["Add a §10.x Estimands section defining the primary estimand and its intercurrent-event strategies (e.g., composite strategy: discontinuation for lack of efficacy or AE, or missing Week 52 biopsy, counted as non-response; treatment-policy strategy for permitted background-medication changes). Define ITT as all randomized subjects. Align sensitivity analyses (tipping point and MNAR) with the estimand.",
  "Prespecify how inadequate biopsies (M-6) and initiation of prohibited NASH therapies such as resmetirom (M-11) are handled."])

H(2, "F. Data Integrity and Electronic Systems")
FINDING("M-3", "No 21 CFR Part 11 provisions for the TrialVault EDC system", "Major",
 "§12.1 (TrialVault described; role-based access, unique login and password, edit checks; no reference to Part 11, validation, audit trail, electronic signatures, backup/recovery)",
 "21 CFR Part 11 (§§11.10(a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (g), (k); 11.50; 11.70; 11.100–11.300); ICH E6(R2) 5.5.3; FDA Guidance, Use of Electronic Records and Electronic Signatures in Clinical Investigations Under 21 CFR Part 11 — Questions and Answers (Oct. 2024 final); Minutes §5 (“Electronic Data Capture”)",
 "FDA reminded Pinnacle that EDC systems must comply with Part 11, be validated, and keep audit trails. Section 12.1 does not mention Part 11. It says nothing about system validation (§11.10(a)), computer-generated time-stamped audit trails (§11.10(e)), operational and authority checks (§11.10(f)–(g)), electronic signature controls and the signature/record linkage (§§11.50, 11.70, 11.100–11.300, including the certification to FDA under §11.100(c)), backup and recovery, or blinding safeguards in the EDC. It also does not address other computerized systems that generate trial records: the IRT (Meridian), central laboratory (Greystone), central pathology, ePRO/injection diaries if electronic, and FibroScan data transfer. The working checklist items 312-035 and GCP-012 remain unassessed.",
 "Part 11 gaps are a frequent BIMO inspection finding. They can render electronic records unreliable for submission. They are unlikely to cause a hold, but they are a material data-integrity risk.",
 ["Add Part 11 language to §12.1 (below). Obtain from Trident the TrialVault validation summary, audit-trail specification and Part 11 assessment before first enrollment. Confirm Pinnacle’s §11.100(c) e-signature certification letter is on file with FDA.",
  "Extend vendor qualification and Part 11 assessments to the IRT, central lab and pathology systems."],
 "12.1.x Electronic Records and Signatures. TrialVault and all other computerized systems used to create, modify, maintain, archive, retrieve or transmit study records (including the IRT, central laboratory and central pathology systems) will comply with 21 CFR Part 11 and ICH E6(R2) Section 5.5.3. Before first data entry, Trident CRO will document validation of TrialVault for its intended use. TrialVault maintains secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails recording the date, time, user and reason for every creation, modification or deletion of data. Audit trails cannot be altered by users and will be retained for the record retention period. Previously recorded information is never obscured. Access is restricted to authorized individuals through unique credentials and role-based permissions, with a current list of individuals authorized to make data changes. Electronic signatures are unique to each individual, linked to their records, and executed in accordance with 21 CFR 11.50, 11.70 and 11.100–11.300. Data will be backed up at least [daily] with documented, tested recovery procedures. EDC configuration will preserve the blind.")

H(2, "G. Multinational Compliance — Health Canada")
FINDING("M-2", "Protocol does not address the Canadian regulatory framework for the six Canadian sites", "Major",
 "§2.2 (lists U.S. regulations only); §11.2 (one sentence on REBs); §12.3 (2-year retention); §13.1 (IND only; 30-day wait for U.S. sites only); §13 (no Canadian content); App. A (U.S.-only ICF: Ridgeway IRB contact, FDA only, English only); App. F (Sites 023–028: Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, Calgary, Ottawa, Edmonton)",
 "Food and Drugs Act; Food and Drug Regulations, Part C, Division 5 (C.05.001–C.05.017), including C.05.005 (CTA), C.05.006 (30-day review and No Objection Letter), C.05.008 (amendments), C.05.010 (sponsor obligations: GCP, REB approval, informed consent, Qualified Investigator), C.05.011 (labelling), C.05.012 (records), C.05.014 (ADR reporting), C.05.015 (discontinuation); ICH E6(R2) as adopted by Health Canada; TCPS 2 (where applicable); Civil Code of Québec arts. 20–24 and Charter of the French Language; provincial health-privacy statutes",
 "The engagement letter (§II.B.12, §II.C.6) asks whether the Protocol can support a CTA for the six Canadian sites. In its current form it cannot. The Protocol names only U.S. law. It does not describe the CTA or No Objection Letter (NOL) prerequisite to Canadian site activation; the Qualified Investigator Undertaking, REB Attestation and Clinical Trial Site Information forms; Health Canada ADR reporting (C.05.014: serious unexpected ADRs within 15 days, fatal or life-threatening within 7 days with a complete report within a further 8 days); bilingual labelling (C.05.011); or Health Canada inspection. Its record-retention period (2 years, §12.3) falls far short of C.05.012(4). We understand that period to be 15 years following the 2022 amendments, which Canadian counsel should confirm. The ICF has no Canadian version: no REB contact, no reference to Health Canada record access, no Canadian privacy-law disclosures, and no French version for Site 025 (Montréal), where Québec law makes French-language consent documentation a practical necessity. There is also a threshold structural decision the Protocol does not make. Canadian sites can be run **under the U.S. IND**, with each Canadian investigator signing Form FDA 1572 and committing to Parts 50, 56 and 312, and each REB having to satisfy Part 56. Or they can be run **outside the IND**, with the data submitted under 21 CFR 312.120 (GCP and independent ethics committee review). The choice affects the 1572s, the REB arrangements, the ICF and the safety reporting.",
 "Health Canada reviews the protocol in the CTA. A protocol that does not acknowledge Division 5 invites a deficiency or a request for a country-specific amendment, and could delay Canadian activation beyond the U.S. start. The 2-year retention clause is incorrect for Canada as written.",
 ["Add the §2.2 and new §13.7 language below. Conform §11.2 (REB), §12.3 (retention: the longer of U.S. and Canadian requirements), §13.1 and §9.1 (Health Canada reporting).",
  "Decide on IND vs. §312.120 status for the Canadian sites, and document the decision in the IND and in §13.7.",
  "Prepare a Canadian ICF version (English and French) with REB contacts, Health Canada access, provincial privacy and injury-coverage language, and Canadian clinical trial insurance confirmation.",
  "Engage Canadian regulatory counsel, as discussed with Dr. Yuen and Dr. Anand. We can make the referral. Under engagement letter §VI, substantial Canadian work beyond this gap analysis may need a scope discussion."],
 ["2.2 (insert after the U.S. regulations list). Canadian Regulatory Framework. At investigational sites in Canada, this study will be conducted in accordance with the Food and Drugs Act and Part C, Division 5 (“Drugs for Clinical Trials Involving Human Subjects”) of the Food and Drug Regulations; the ICH E6(R2) Guideline for Good Clinical Practice as adopted by Health Canada; the Tri-Council Policy Statement: Ethical Conduct for Research Involving Humans (TCPS 2), where applicable; and applicable provincial and territorial laws governing consent to research and the protection of personal health information, including, for sites in Québec, the Civil Code of Québec. The Sponsor will file a Clinical Trial Application (CTA) with Health Canada and will not sell or import study drug for, or begin the study at, any Canadian site until Health Canada has issued a No Objection Letter (or the 30-day review period under C.05.006 has expired without objection) and the site’s Research Ethics Board (REB) has approved the protocol and informed consent form. [Canadian sites will be conducted under IND [number] and each Canadian qualified investigator will also execute Form FDA 1572.]",
  "13.7 Canadian Regulatory Requirements. (a) CTA and amendments: The Sponsor will maintain the CTA and will submit CTA amendments (C.05.008) or notifications (C.05.007), as applicable, for protocol or quality changes; amendments will not be implemented at Canadian sites until Health Canada has issued a No Objection Letter (where required) and REB approval is obtained, except where necessary to eliminate an immediate hazard. (b) Qualified Investigators and REBs: Before site activation, the Sponsor will obtain a Qualified Investigator Undertaking, an REB Attestation and a Clinical Trial Site Information form for each Canadian site. (c) Adverse drug reaction reporting: The Sponsor will report to Health Canada each serious unexpected adverse drug reaction that occurs in Canada or elsewhere (i) within 15 days after becoming aware of it, or (ii) if fatal or life-threatening, within 7 days, followed by a complete report within 8 days thereafter (C.05.014). (d) Labelling: Study drug supplied to Canadian sites will be labelled in English and French in accordance with C.05.011. (e) Records: Records required by C.05.012 will be retained for [15] years. (f) Discontinuation: The Sponsor will notify Health Canada of any discontinuation of the study, in whole or at any site, in accordance with C.05.015. (g) Informed consent: Canadian sites will use a Canadian-specific, REB-approved ICF, in French where required, that discloses access to records by Health Canada and complies with applicable provincial law. FINDING("M-9", "ICF duration and procedure descriptions are inaccurate or incomplete", "Major",
 "App. A §A2 (“Your participation in this study will last approximately 12 months”; follow-up visits not counted; one baseline biopsy); compare Table 1 and §5.1 (64 weeks from randomization; 72 weeks including screening), §6.3 (possible fresh baseline biopsy), §3.3 (MRI-PDFF subset; PROs)",
 "21 CFR 50.25(a)(1); ICH E6(R2) 4.8.10(d), (f), (s)",
 "The statement that participation lasts “approximately 12 months” describes only the 52-week treatment period, which is about 12 months. Participation actually runs about **64 weeks (about 15 months) after randomization and up to 72 weeks (about 16.5 months) including screening**. The ICF should not say “16 months” for 64 weeks; that conversion is inaccurate. The ICF also (i) does not say how many follow-up visits there are (three, at Weeks 56, 60 and 64) or that they are about 4 weeks apart; (ii) does not disclose that a subject may need a **second pre-treatment biopsy** if the qualifying biopsy is more than 4 weeks old (§6.3), or a repeat biopsy if a specimen is inadequate (M-6); (iii) does not identify which procedures are experimental or done only for research, as §50.25(a)(1) requires (for example, the Week 52 biopsy is done for research); (iv) does not mention the MRI-PDFF sub-study, the patient-reported outcome questionnaires, the injection diary, or the PK sampling with timed post-dose draws (and the longer visits at PK-intensive sites); and (v) does not mention the Week 52 visit window or what happens if study drug is stopped early (subjects are asked to stay in the study and still have the Week 52 biopsy, §4.3).",
 "An inaccurate duration is a misstatement of a basic element. IRBs and FDA treat it as such, and it was the specific issue Ms. Kowalski raised.",
 ["Replace the duration sentence (below). Add a visit-by-visit summary table in lay terms. Identify research-only procedures. Describe the possible additional biopsies, MRI-PDFF (optional or site-specific), PROs, PK sampling and the injection diary."],
 "“If you join the study, you will be in it for up to about 16½ months (up to 72 weeks). This includes up to 8 weeks of screening tests, 52 weeks (about 1 year) of study drug or placebo injections, and 12 weeks of follow-up visits after your last injection. You will have about 17 study visits, including the screening visit.”")

FINDING("M-10", "ICF risk disclosure is incomplete", "Major",
 "App. A §A3 (biopsy: bleeding, infection, pain, organ puncture; drug: GI, injection site, pancreatitis, thyroid tumors, hypoglycemia, unknown risks; blood draws)",
 "21 CFR 50.25(a)(2), (b)(1); ICH E6(R2) 4.8.10(g); Protocol §9.2 (AESIs), §9.5.1 (stopping criteria)",
 "The ICF leaves out reasonably foreseeable risks that the Protocol itself identifies or monitors: (i) **liver injury and worsening liver disease**, including the hepatic decompensation events that are AESIs and the focus of FDA’s stopping criteria (§9.2(1), (5); §9.5); (ii) **serious allergic reactions and anaphylaxis**, which are a stopping criterion (§9.5.1(3)); (iii) dehydration and kidney injury from GI fluid loss; (iv) gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis and cholecystitis), a recognized incretin class effect, and increased heart rate; (v) pneumothorax and the rare risk of death from liver biopsy, plus aspiration risk if sedation is used, given delayed gastric emptying with this drug class; (vi) reproductive risks (C-7); (vii) the risk of the liver disease progressing while on placebo or an ineffective dose, and of temporarily stopping prohibited medicines; (viii) minor risks of ECG, FibroScan and MRI; and (ix) loss of confidentiality, including genetic information (M-12). The working checklist marked §50.25(a)(2) “Y” (IC-002) and recorded “Phase 1 findings” and “theoretical hepatotoxicity risk noted” (IC-025). Neither appears in this ICF, and PTX-4820 has no Phase 1 data of its own.",
 "An incomplete risk disclosure is a substantive defect in a basic element. Both IRBs and FDA review the ICF risk section against the IB and the protocol’s own safety monitoring.",
 "Revise §A3 against the current IB Reference Safety Information and Protocol §9.2/§9.5, with input from Dr. Anand. Add the risks listed above in lay terms, and keep the risk section consistent with future IB updates."
)

FINDING("M-11", "Protocol and ICF misstate that no therapy is approved for NASH with F2–F3 fibrosis", "Major",
 "§2.1 (“there are currently no pharmacotherapies approved by the U.S. FDA specifically for the treatment of NASH with liver fibrosis, as of the date of this protocol”); §2.1 Orphan Drug paragraph (“absence of approved therapies”); App. A §A5 (“Currently, there is no FDA-approved drug treatment specifically for NASH with liver fibrosis”); §5.4 (prohibited medications)",
 "21 CFR 50.25(a)(4); 21 CFR 312.23(a)(6); ICH E6(R2) 4.8.10(i); ICH E10 (choice of control group)",
 "On March 14, 2024, more than a year before the Protocol date, FDA granted accelerated approval to **resmetirom (Rezdiffra)** for adults with noncirrhotic NASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis (consistent with F2–F3), used with diet and exercise. content.text:
I wrote and validated the gap analysis memo. It concludes that Protocol PTX-4820-201 v3.0 and its consent form are not ready to file for the September 15, 2025 IND. The memo has 33 findings (10 Critical, 13 Major, 10 Minor, plus 1 observation outside scope). Each has a regulatory citation and a recommended fix, and most include proposed protocol or consent-form wording. The core problems:
- **Pre-IND action items:** none of the six revisions agreed with FDA in the April 2, 2025 meeting minutes have been made (mandatory DSMB, two-reader pathology, study-level stopping rules, interim and futility analysis, MELD ≥15 exclusion, 4-week titration of the 30 mg dose). The biopsy-adequacy commitment is also not met.
- **Consent form:** it is missing three required elements: confidentiality and FDA inspection, compensation for research injury, and the ClinicalTrials.gov statement. It also says the study lasts "approximately 12 months"; it is about 15 months from randomization, or about 16.5 months including screening.
- **Pregnancy protections:** there are no contraception, pregnancy-testing or pregnancy/breastfeeding exclusion provisions.
- **Other gaps:**
  - Expedited safety-reporting timelines are not stated.
  - Health Canada and Canadian site requirements are not addressed; wording for Sections 2.2 and a new 13.7 is drafted.
  - The data system (TrialVault) is not described against 21 CFR Part 11.
  - Nothing stops dosing past Week 26 before the required 39-week toxicology results are in.
  - Liver lab monitoring is less frequent than FDA recommended.
  - There is no estimand framework.

Four points go beyond what the inputs said:
- **Sample size:** on my own calculation, the stated assumptions need about 163 evaluable subjects per arm, not 78. At 90 per arm the study has roughly 48% power, not 80%. This could change the trial's size and budget, so Pinnacle's biostatistician should confirm it before anyone relies on it.
- **Approved therapy:** both the protocol and the consent form say no drug is approved for this condition. That is wrong: FDA approved resmetirom (Rezdiffra) for this population on March 14, 2024. This rests on my own knowledge, not the documents, so please verify it.
- **Working checklist:** many of its "compliant" entries describe a different protocol (version 2.0, 50/150/300 mg doses, a DSMB that v3.0 does not have). The memo states that a corrected checklist will be delivered by July 11. That is a commitment the firm still has to fulfil; I did not produce it here.
- **Corrections to the firm's June 18 email:** 64 weeks is about 15 months, not 16. Section 13 of the protocol does not mention the Canadian sites at all.

I dated the memo July 9, 2025, to fit the engagement timeline. The Canadian points (record retention of 15 years, French-language consent for Québec) are flagged in the memo for Canadian counsel to confirm.
